short: heel pain, arch pain, and morning heel pain
lead: Heel pain and arch pain are common ways the foot tells you something is overloaded or irritated. The pain can come from the heel bone, the thick band under the foot, a tendon, or a nerve. Many people notice it most with the first steps after getting out of bed.
Adults, active kids, and people who stand for work all get these pains. Finding the true source early often keeps a small problem from turning into a long one.
feels: Sharp or stabbing pain in the heel with the first steps of the day
An ache along the arch that grows by evening
Pain that eases after walking a bit, then returns after rest
Tenderness when you press on the bottom or back of the heel
causes: Long hours standing or walking on hard floors
Shoes with weak support or worn-out soles
Sudden jumps in exercise or training
Tight calf muscles or flat or high arches
diagnose: We start by asking when the pain hits and where it sits. Then we press on the heel and arch, check how your foot moves, and look at how you walk. X-rays can show the heel bone, and ultrasound or MRI may be used if a tendon or soft tissue problem is suspected.
treat: Most heel and arch pain improves without surgery. Stretching the calf and the arch, wearing supportive shoes, and cutting back on the activity that flares it are good first steps. We may add taping, custom orthotics, physical therapy, or shockwave therapy. Injections are sometimes used for stubborn pain.
more: Surgery is rarely needed and is only considered when months of good non-surgical care have not helped. The type of procedure depends on what is causing the pain.
recovery: Many people feel clearly better within a few weeks to a few months of steady care. Pain that has lasted a long time can take longer to settle, and it may come back if the causes stay the same.
when: See a podiatrist if heel pain lasts more than a couple of weeks or keeps you from your normal day. Come sooner if you have swelling, numbness, or pain that wakes you at night.

faqs.q: Why does my heel hurt most when I first get up?
faqs.a: Tissue in the foot tightens while you rest, so the first steps pull on sore spots. The pain often eases as the foot warms up.

faqs.q: Should I keep walking on a painful heel?
faqs.a: Gentle activity is usually fine, but pushing through sharp pain can make things worse. A podiatrist can tell you what level of activity is safe.

title: Heel Pain, Arch Pain & Morning Heel Pain

short: plantar fasciitis and chronic plantar fasciosis
lead: The plantar fascia is a strong band that runs from your heel to your toes and supports the arch. When it is overloaded, it can become sore and inflamed, which is called plantar fasciitis. If the problem lasts for months, the tissue can wear down and thicken, and this is called plantar fasciosis.
It is one of the most common causes of heel pain and shows up in runners, teachers, nurses, and many others. Starting care early can help stop a short flare from becoming a long-term problem.
feels: Stabbing pain in the bottom of the heel with first steps
Pain after standing up from a long time sitting
Soreness that builds during long days on your feet
A tight, pulling feeling along the arch
causes: Repeated strain from running, jumping, or long standing
Tight calf muscles and a stiff Achilles tendon
Flat feet, high arches, or unusual foot mechanics
Extra body weight or sudden weight change
diagnose: We look for pain at the spot where the band meets the heel and check how tight your calf and foot are. An X-ray can rule out a stress fracture or other bone problem. Ultrasound can show a thickened fascia, especially when the pain has lasted a long time.
treat: Care starts with daily stretches for the calf and the bottom of the foot, plus shoes with good cushion and arch support. Night splints, taping, and custom orthotics can take strain off the band. Physical therapy helps build strength and flexibility. For pain that will not settle, shockwave therapy or an injection may be options.
more: Surgery is uncommon and is usually kept for pain that lasts many months despite steady non-surgical care. A procedure may release part of the fascia to reduce tension.
recovery: Most people improve over several weeks to a few months. Chronic cases can take six months or longer, and staying with the stretching plan helps keep pain from returning.
when: Book a visit if your heel pain has lasted more than two weeks or is getting worse. Do not wait if you cannot walk normally or the heel is swollen, red, or numb.

faqs.q: What is the difference between fasciitis and fasciosis?
faqs.a: Fasciitis usually means a newer, inflamed band. Fasciosis means long-term wear and thickening of the tissue, which often needs a longer plan.

faqs.q: Will a cortisone shot fix it for good?
faqs.a: An injection can calm pain for a time, but it does not fix the reasons the band is overloaded. It works best alongside stretching, support, and activity changes.

title: Plantar Fasciitis & Chronic Plantar Fasciosis

lead: A heel spur is a small, bony bump that grows on the underside of the heel bone. It forms slowly, often over months or years, as the body reacts to steady pulling on the foot's tissues. Many spurs are seen on X-rays in people who feel nothing at all.

Spurs are more common in adults and in people who run, stand a lot, or have plantar fasciitis. The pain people feel usually comes from the irritated tissue nearby, and treating that tissue early often brings relief.
feels: Pain at the bottom of the heel when you stand or walk
A feeling like a small stone under the heel
Tenderness when you press on the front of the heel
Soreness that is worse after rest or long activity
causes: Long-term pulling of the foot's supporting band on the heel bone
Repeated impact from running or hard-surface work
Tight calves and stiff feet
Poorly fitting shoes or worn-out footwear
diagnose: A weight-bearing X-ray is the best way to see a spur, and it also shows the shape of the heel bone. We check where it hurts, because the spur itself is often not the source of pain. This helps us tell whether the true problem is the nearby fascia or another condition.
treat: Treatment aims at the sore tissue around the spur. Padded heel cups, custom orthotics, and roomy, cushioned shoes reduce pressure on the bone. Stretching, physical therapy, and taping can ease pulling on the heel. Shockwave therapy or an injection may be tried when pain lingers.
more: Surgery to remove a spur is rare and is only considered after a long trial of other care. The bump does not need to be removed just because it appears on an X-ray.
recovery: Most people feel better over weeks to a few months once the irritated tissue calms down. The spur usually stays on the X-ray, but pain can still go away.
when: See us if heel pain keeps returning or lasts longer than two weeks. Get checked promptly if the heel looks red, feels hot, or hurts even at rest.

faqs.q: Do heel spurs go away on their own?
faqs.a: The bone itself does not shrink, but the pain often fades with care. Many people live comfortably with a spur.

faqs.q: Do I need surgery to remove the spur?
faqs.a: Most people do not. Pain is usually managed by treating the soft tissue and easing pressure on the heel.

title: Heel Spurs (Calcaneal Spurs)

lead: The Achilles tendon connects your calf muscles to your heel bone. When it is overworked, it can become sore and swollen, which is tendinitis. If the strain continues, the tendon fibers can weaken and thicken, which is called tendinosis. The trouble can be in the middle of the tendon or right where it attaches to the heel.
It often affects runners, weekend athletes, and adults who are on their feet a lot. Because tendons heal slowly, getting help early can protect you from a tear later.
feels: Aching or stiffness in the back of the heel or lower calf
Morning stiffness that eases as you warm up
A thickened or swollen spot along the tendon
Pain that returns after running, stairs, or uphill walking
causes: Doing too much, too soon in sports or training
Tight calf muscles that pull on the tendon
Rubbing from stiff heel counters in shoes
Foot alignment that changes how the tendon is loaded
diagnose: We feel along the tendon to find the tender or thick area and test calf strength and flexibility. Ultrasound is useful for seeing changes inside the tendon. X-rays show whether a bone bump is involved at the heel, and MRI may be advised in tough cases.
treat: The key is to reduce the load without stopping all movement. Heel lifts, supportive shoes, and short-term boots or bracing can ease strain. Slow, guided strengthening with physical therapy is often the most helpful step for a sore tendon. Orthotics may help if foot mechanics are adding stress. Shockwave therapy is another option for long-lasting pain.
more: Surgery is uncommon and is considered when many months of care have not worked. It may involve cleaning out damaged tendon tissue or, for the insertional type, smoothing bone at the heel.
recovery: Mild cases can settle in several weeks. Tendinosis often takes three to six months or more, so patience and steady exercises matter.
when: Make an appointment if back-of-heel pain lasts more than a week or two or keeps you from exercise. Come in right away if you hear a pop or suddenly cannot push off your foot.

faqs.q: Is it safe to keep running with Achilles pain?
faqs.a: Mild pain may allow lighter activity, but pushing through it can worsen the tendon. We can help you set safe limits.

faqs.q: What is the difference between insertional and non-insertional?
faqs.a: Insertional problems sit where the tendon meets the heel bone. Non-insertional problems affect the middle of the tendon, a bit higher up.

title: Achilles Tendinitis & Tendinosis (Insertional and Non-Insertional)

lead: An Achilles tear happens when the big tendon at the back of the ankle is partly or fully torn. A full tear is also called a rupture. It can happen suddenly during sport or a quick push-off, and it can make walking hard right away.
These injuries are most common in adults who play stop-and-go sports, often in their 30s to 50s. Quick care matters, because the right plan is easier to start soon after the injury.
feels: A sudden pop or snap at the back of the ankle
Sharp pain, as if someone kicked your calf
Trouble rising onto your toes or pushing off
Swelling and bruising behind the ankle
causes: Sudden bursts of effort in sports like basketball or tennis
Long-term tendon wear that weakens the fibers
A missed step or a fall that stretches the tendon
Some medicines and past injections near the tendon
diagnose: We check for a gap in the tendon and test how the foot moves when we squeeze the calf. Ultrasound is often used to see how much of the tendon is torn. MRI can add detail in unclear or partial tears.
treat: Some tears are treated without surgery. This usually means a boot or cast that holds the foot in a helpful position, followed by careful physical therapy. The right approach depends on the tear, your age, your activity level, and your health. We talk through the options so you can choose with confidence.
more: Surgery may be recommended to repair the tendon, especially for active people or larger tears. Both surgery and non-surgical care can work well, and each has its own risks.
recovery: Healing takes time, often six months to a year before full return to sport. Most people walk normally well before that, but strength builds slowly.
when: Get seen as soon as possible if you think you tore your Achilles. Until then, keep weight off the foot and avoid stretching the area.

faqs.q: Can I walk with a torn Achilles?
faqs.a: Some people can still walk, but usually with a limp and weak push-off. Walking does not mean the tendon is fine, so it should still be checked.

faqs.q: Is a partial tear less serious?
faqs.a: It is often easier to manage, but it can still worsen if ignored. Ultrasound or MRI helps us plan the right care.

title: Achilles Tendon Tears & Ruptures

lead: A bursa is a small fluid-filled cushion that helps tissues glide over bone. When one becomes irritated and swollen, the problem is called bursitis. In the heel, this can happen behind the bone near the Achilles tendon (retrocalcaneal) or under the heel (plantar).
It is often seen in active people and in those whose shoes rub or press on the heel. Easing the pressure early can keep the cushion from staying inflamed.
feels: Deep pain behind the heel, just in front of the Achilles
Tenderness under the heel when you step down
Puffiness or warmth around the back of the heel
Pain when you rise onto your toes or wear tight shoes
causes: Rubbing from stiff or narrow shoe backs
Repeated impact from running or jumping
Tight Achilles and calf muscles
A prominent heel bone that pinches the bursa
diagnose: We press around the back and underside of the heel to find the sore spot and look for swelling. Ultrasound can show fluid in the bursa. X-rays help us check the shape of the heel bone, and MRI is used when the picture is unclear.
treat: Relief starts with taking pressure off the bursa. Softer shoes with a padded or open back, heel lifts, and small cushions can help a lot. Rest from high-impact exercise, calf stretching, and physical therapy are common parts of care. In some cases, an injection is used to calm a flared bursa.
more: Surgery is rare. If pain stays after a long period of good care, a procedure may remove the irritated bursa or smooth a bony bump that is pressing on it.
recovery: Many people feel better in a few weeks to a couple of months. It may take longer if shoe rubbing or heavy activity keeps irritating the area.
when: See a podiatrist if heel swelling or pain lasts more than a couple of weeks. Seek care quickly if the area turns red, hot, or very painful, since infection is possible.

faqs.q: Is bursitis the same as Achilles tendinitis?
faqs.a: No, though they can occur together. Bursitis affects the cushion, while tendinitis affects the tendon itself.

faqs.q: Can shoes make heel bursitis worse?
faqs.a: Yes, stiff heel backs and tight fits can rub and press on the bursa. Changing shoes is often a big part of relief.

title: Retrocalcaneal & Plantar Heel Bursitis

lead: Haglund's deformity is a bony bump on the back of the heel, where the Achilles tendon attaches. It is often called a pump bump because stiff dress shoes and pumps tend to rub against it. The bump can irritate the skin, the tendon, and the small cushion nearby.
It is seen in teens and adults, and it can run in families with certain heel shapes. Early changes in footwear can stop the rubbing before it becomes a constant problem.
feels: A hard bump on the back of the heel
Redness or a blister where the shoe rubs
Pain or swelling at the back of the heel when walking
Soreness that is worse in closed-back shoes
causes: A heel bone shape that sticks out at the back
Stiff shoe backs that press on the bump
A high arch that tilts the heel outward
Tight Achilles tendon that adds pressure
diagnose: We look at the back of the heel, feel the bump, and check the Achilles tendon for irritation. A side-view X-ray shows the shape of the heel bone. Ultrasound or MRI may be added to see if the tendon or bursa is inflamed.
treat: Changing shoes is often the biggest help. Open-back or soft-heeled shoes, heel pads with a cut-out, and heel lifts reduce rubbing. Stretching, physical therapy, and orthotics can lower strain on the tendon. Ice and short-term anti-inflammatory care can calm a flare.
more: If pain stays despite good non-surgical care, surgery can trim the bump and treat any tendon damage. The plan depends on how much of the tendon is involved.
recovery: Symptoms can settle in weeks to a few months with better shoes and care. After surgery, recovery is longer and often takes several months.
when: Come in if the bump keeps hurting, blistering, or swelling. Do not wait if you see open skin, spreading redness, or fever.

faqs.q: Will the bump go away with treatment?
faqs.a: The bone bump usually stays, but the pain and swelling can improve a lot. Surgery is the only way to remove the bone.

faqs.q: Do I have to stop wearing my work shoes?
faqs.a: Not always. Small changes like heel pads or a softer back can make many shoes more comfortable.

title: Haglund's Deformity ("Pump Bump")

lead: Under your heel bone sits a thick pad of fat that absorbs shock with every step. If it is bruised, inflamed, or worn thin, the heel loses its cushion. Doctors call this heel fat pad syndrome, and thinning over time is called fat pad atrophy.
It is more common in older adults, runners, and people who walk barefoot on hard floors. Since the pain can look like other heel problems, a proper exam helps you get the right plan.
feels: Deep, bruise-like pain in the middle of the heel
Pain when you walk barefoot or on hard floors
The heel feels thin or hard underneath
Soreness that gets worse as the day goes on
causes: Natural thinning of the heel pad with age
Repeated hard landings from running or jumping
A hard blow to the heel, such as a fall
Long stretches of walking without cushioned shoes
diagnose: We press on the center of the heel and feel how thick and firm the pad is. Ultrasound can show the pad and measure its thickness. X-rays help rule out a stress fracture or a heel spur as the source.
treat: Care focuses on giving the heel its cushion back. Shoes with a thick, soft sole, gel or foam heel cups, and orthotics with heel padding spread out the impact. We may suggest less running on hard ground and walking with shoes at home. Taping can also help hold the pad in place.
more: Surgery is not common for this condition. A few advanced options exist for severe cases, but padding and activity changes work for most people.
recovery: If the pad is bruised, it may improve over several weeks to a few months. A pad that has thinned with age will not grow back, but cushioning can keep you comfortable.
when: See a podiatrist if deep heel pain lasts more than a couple of weeks or makes walking hard. Come promptly after a hard fall on the heel or if there is bruising or swelling.

faqs.q: How is this different from plantar fasciitis?
faqs.a: Fat pad pain tends to be in the center of the heel and feels like a bruise. Plantar fasciitis is usually felt toward the inside front of the heel, with first-step pain.

faqs.q: Can the fat pad grow back?
faqs.a: Usually not once it has thinned. Good cushioning and supportive shoes protect the heel instead.

title: Heel Fat Pad Syndrome & Fat Pad Atrophy

lead: A calcaneal stress fracture is a tiny crack in the heel bone, caused by repeated stress rather than one big injury. The heel bone takes a lot of force with every step, so it can wear down if it does not get time to recover. Small cracks can grow if you keep pushing through the pain.
It often affects runners, military recruits, dancers, and people who suddenly raise their activity. Catching it early helps the bone heal and lowers the chance of a longer break from activity.
feels: Deep heel pain that builds with running or jumping
Pain when you squeeze the sides of the heel
Swelling or warmth around the heel bone
Aching even at rest in more advanced cases
causes: A fast jump in mileage or training time
Hard surfaces or worn-out running shoes
Low bone strength or low vitamin D
Not enough rest between hard workouts
diagnose: We check for pain when the sides of the heel are squeezed and ask about recent changes in training. Early stress fractures may not show on an X-ray, so MRI is often the best test. CT can help in special cases, and blood tests may be used to check bone health.
treat: The main treatment is rest from the activity that caused it. A walking boot or crutches takes weight off the bone while it heals. We build a slow return plan and may suggest cross-training like swimming or cycling. Shoes with good cushion and, at times, orthotics reduce future stress.
more: Surgery is rarely needed for stress fractures of the heel. It is considered only if the bone fails to heal or the fracture shifts.
recovery: Healing often takes six to twelve weeks, and return to running is gradual after that. Coming back too soon can set healing back.
when: See a podiatrist if heel pain keeps building with activity or hurts when you squeeze the heel. Stop hard exercise until you are seen, since a small crack can grow.

faqs.q: Why did my X-ray look normal?
faqs.a: Early stress fractures are often too small to see on an X-ray. MRI can show the injury much sooner.

faqs.q: Can I keep training while it heals?
faqs.a: Usually not on the injured heel. Low-impact options like swimming may be possible if we approve them.

title: Calcaneal (Heel Bone) Stress Fractures

lead: Sever's disease is heel pain in growing kids, caused by irritation of the growth plate at the back of the heel bone. The growth plate is a soft area where new bone forms, and the Achilles tendon pulls on it. It is a common overuse problem and not a sign of lasting damage.
It usually appears in active children between about 8 and 14. Simple steps taken early can help your child stay in the game with less pain.
feels: Heel pain during or after sports and running
Limping or walking on tiptoes to avoid heel pressure
Soreness when the sides of the heel are squeezed
Pain that eases with rest and returns with play
causes: Fast growth that leaves calf muscles tight
Lots of running and jumping on hard surfaces
Cleats or shoes with little heel cushion
Flat feet or foot alignment that adds strain
diagnose: We ask about your child's sports and shoes, then check the heel, calf flexibility, and foot shape. The squeeze test is a simple way to spot growth plate irritation. An X-ray can rule out a fracture or other problem, though it does not usually show Sever's itself.
treat: Relief comes from easing the pull on the heel. Heel cups or lifts, supportive shoes, and calf stretches are the core of care. Kids may need to cut back on sports for a while, and ice after play can help. Orthotics or taping are options for those with flat feet or ongoing pain.
more: Surgery is not used for Sever's disease. It settles as the growth plate matures.
recovery: Most children feel better within a few weeks to a few months. Pain can return during growth spurts but usually ends once growth is complete.
when: Book a visit if your child limps, complains of heel pain after sports, or has pain that lasts more than a week or two. Come in quickly if there is swelling, a fall, or pain at night.

faqs.q: Does my child have to quit sports?
faqs.a: Often not fully. Cutting back, using heel support, and stretching may let your child keep playing with less pain.

faqs.q: Will Sever's disease cause problems as an adult?
faqs.a: It does not usually cause lasting harm. It goes away once the heel bone finishes growing.

title: Sever's Disease (Calcaneal Apophysitis)

lead: A bunion is a bony bump on the inside of the foot at the base of the big toe. It forms when the big toe leans toward the second toe and the joint shifts out of line. Over time, the bump can grow, and the joint can get sore and stiff.
Bunions can run in families and are seen in adults and in teens. Getting a look early lets us slow the change and pick the best time to act.
feels: A firm bump on the inside of the big toe joint
Redness, swelling, or soreness over the bump
Pain when wearing narrow or tight shoes
A big toe that drifts toward the other toes
causes: Inherited foot shape and loose joints
Narrow shoes and high heels that squeeze the toes
Flat feet that roll inward
Joint or arthritis conditions that change foot alignment
diagnose: We look at how the big toe sits, how the joint moves, and how you walk. Weight-bearing X-rays measure the angle of the toe and the joint so we can see how much it has shifted. This helps us decide between shoe and support changes or a surgical plan.
treat: Wider shoes with a soft, roomy toe box are the first step. Bunion pads, toe spacers, and custom orthotics can ease pressure and pain. Icing and, at times, an injection can calm a sore joint. Care can ease symptoms, but it does not straighten a bunion.
more: Surgery is an option when pain limits daily life despite good non-surgical care. There are several types of bunion procedures, and we match the choice to your foot and your goals.
recovery: After surgery, most people spend several weeks protecting the foot and return to regular shoes within about two to three months. Full healing can take longer, and results vary from person to person.
when: See a podiatrist if a bunion hurts, rubs, or makes shoe fitting hard. Also come in if the toe is crowding others or a teen shows early signs.

faqs.q: Can I get rid of a bunion without surgery?
faqs.a: Non-surgical care can lower pain but cannot straighten the bone. Surgery is the only way to correct the alignment.

faqs.q: Do teens get bunions?
faqs.a: Yes, some teens develop them, often because of family foot shape. Early checks help us guide shoes and support.

title: Bunions (Hallux Valgus) in Adults & Adolescents

short: big toe arthritis, hallux limitus, and hallux rigidus
lead: Hallux limitus and hallux rigidus are forms of arthritis in the joint at the base of the big toe. In hallux limitus, the toe bends less than it should. In hallux rigidus, the joint becomes very stiff, and bone spurs often form on top.
This tends to affect adults, though it can begin earlier after an injury or in people with certain foot shapes. Since the big toe bends with every step, treating it early can protect how you walk.
feels: Stiffness and pain at the base of the big toe
Trouble bending the toe when walking or climbing stairs
A bump on top of the big toe joint
Aching that flares in cold or damp weather
causes: Wear and tear on the joint over many years
A past injury like a stubbed or jammed toe
Family history of arthritis or foot shape that overloads the joint
Jobs or sports with lots of squatting or push-off
diagnose: We check how far the big toe bends and whether the joint feels sore or grinds. Weight-bearing X-rays show narrowing of the joint space and any bone spurs. This tells us how far the arthritis has advanced.
treat: Stiff-soled or rocker-bottom shoes can reduce bending and pain. Custom orthotics, a shoe insert that supports the toe, and physical therapy can help. Injections may calm a flare. We also suggest activity changes that keep you moving without pressing on the joint.
more: When pain is strong and other care does not help, surgery may be offered. Options range from cleaning up bone spurs to fusing or replacing the joint, depending on how advanced the arthritis is.
recovery: With non-surgical care, many people find steady relief over weeks to months, though the joint stays stiff. After surgery, expect several weeks of protected walking and a few months before full comfort.
when: See a podiatrist if your big toe hurts with walking or keeps getting stiffer. Come in sooner if you have swelling, redness, or pain at rest.

faqs.q: Is hallux rigidus the same as a bunion?
faqs.a: No. A bunion is a shift of the toe, while hallux rigidus is arthritis with stiffness in the joint. They can occur in the same foot.

faqs.q: Will the arthritis keep getting worse?
faqs.a: It can progress slowly over time. Good shoes and early care may help slow the trouble and keep you active.

title: Hallux Limitus, Hallux Rigidus & Big Toe Arthritis

lead: Hallux varus is when the big toe drifts toward the inside of the foot, away from the other toes. It is the opposite of a bunion, where the toe leans toward the second toe. It can make shoes hard to fit and may cause pain or trouble balancing.
It is rare. It may be present from birth in some children, or it can develop in adults after bunion surgery or an injury. A careful check helps us find the cause and plan the right care.
feels: The big toe points inward, with a gap between it and the second toe
Rubbing or pain on the side of the big toe in shoes
Trouble finding shoes that fit well
Stiffness or pain in the big toe joint
causes: Over-correction after bunion surgery
Being born with an unusual toe shape or tendon pull
Injury to the big toe joint or its supporting tissue
Conditions like arthritis or nerve problems that change toe position
diagnose: We look at the shape and position of the big toe and test how the joint moves. We also learn if the toe can be moved back into place by hand. Weight-bearing X-rays show the angle of the joint and any changes in the bone.
treat: If the toe is flexible and not very painful, non-surgical care is often enough. Roomy shoes with a wide toe box, toe spacers, padding, and taping can ease rubbing. Custom orthotics and physical therapy may help with balance and foot mechanics. Bracing can hold the toe in a better position for some people.
more: If the toe is stiff, painful, or interferes with walking, surgery may be considered. The procedure is chosen based on whether the joint is flexible or fixed and what caused the problem.
recovery: Recovery depends on the care chosen. Non-surgical approaches may improve comfort within weeks, while surgery often needs about two to three months before regular shoes feel comfortable.
when: See a podiatrist if your big toe drifts inward or you notice a change after foot surgery. Come in earlier if the toe is painful, rubs, or affects your balance.

faqs.q: Can hallux varus happen after bunion surgery?
faqs.a: Yes, in some cases the toe shifts too far the other way. Telling us about past surgery helps us plan care.

faqs.q: Is a child born with hallux varus treated differently?
faqs.a: Yes. Children may respond to gentle stretching, splinting, or watchful waiting, and we tailor the plan to age and growth.

title: Hallux Varus

lead: The sesamoids are two tiny bones under the big toe joint that act like pulleys for a tendon. Sesamoiditis means these bones and the tendon around them are irritated. A sesamoid can also crack, and in rare cases the bone can lose blood supply, which is called avascular necrosis (AVN).
These problems are common in runners, dancers, and people who spend time on the balls of their feet. Early care can protect the bones and help you avoid long-lasting pain.
feels: Pain under the ball of the foot, below the big toe
Aching that gets worse when you push off or squat
Swelling or a sore spot under the big toe joint
Pain when bending the big toe up or down
causes: Repeated pressure from running, jumping, or dancing
Wearing high heels or thin, flat shoes
A high arch that puts weight on the ball of the foot
A sudden injury such as a hard landing
diagnose: We press under the big toe joint and test how the toe moves against resistance. X-rays show the sesamoids and whether one is cracked. MRI or a CT referral may be used to look for bone stress, a loss of blood flow, or an injury not seen on X-ray.
treat: Taking weight off the sesamoids is the key. Cushioned shoes, a padded insert that gives the area a dip, and stiff-soled footwear help. A walking boot or taping may be needed for a period of time. Anti-inflammatory care, physical therapy, and an injection can also be part of the plan.
more: Surgery is not common but may be advised for a fracture that does not heal or for AVN. The procedure may remove all or part of the sesamoid.
recovery: Simple irritation often improves in several weeks to a few months. Fractures and blood flow problems can take longer, sometimes several months.
when: See a podiatrist if pain under the big toe lasts more than a week or two or came on after a fall or jump. Come sooner if you cannot bear weight or the joint swells.

faqs.q: How can I tell if it is sesamoiditis or a fracture?
faqs.a: The pain can feel alike, so an exam and X-ray are needed. MRI may be added when the answer is unclear.

faqs.q: What does AVN mean for the sesamoid?
faqs.a: It means part of the bone has lost blood flow and may weaken. It is uncommon and is watched closely with imaging.

title: Sesamoiditis, Sesamoid Fractures & AVN

lead: A tailor's bunion is a bump on the outside of the foot, at the base of the little toe. It forms when the small toe bone shifts inward and the joint sticks out. It is also called a bunionette.
It is common in people who wear narrow shoes or who were born with a certain foot shape. Early care can keep the bump from growing and rubbing more.
feels: A firm bump on the outer side of the foot
Redness or swelling over the bump
Pain when shoes press on the side of the foot
Thick skin or a corn over the bump
causes: Narrow or pointed shoes that squeeze the toes
An inherited foot shape or bone structure
A loose or unstable joint at the little toe
Long hours on your feet in tight footwear
diagnose: We look at the bump, check how the little toe moves, and see where shoes rub. A weight-bearing X-ray shows the angle of the bone and how far it has shifted. This helps us choose the right plan.
treat: Wider shoes with a roomy toe box are the first step. Soft pads can shield the bump from rubbing, and custom orthotics may ease pressure on the forefoot. If the area is inflamed, ice and a short course of anti-inflammatory care may help. Some patients also benefit from an injection to calm a sore, swollen joint.
more: Surgery is considered when pain continues despite good shoes and other care. The surgeon may reshape or realign the bone so the little toe sits straighter.
recovery: Many people feel better within a few weeks of switching shoes and using pads. After surgery, expect roughly six to twelve weeks before returning to normal shoes, though this varies.
when: See a podiatrist if the bump hurts most days or if a sore keeps forming on it. Get checked sooner if you have diabetes or poor feeling in your feet.

faqs.q: Will a tailor's bunion go away on its own?
faqs.a: The bone shift does not reverse without surgery. Pain and rubbing can often be managed well with shoe changes and pads.

faqs.q: Are bunions and tailor's bunions the same?
faqs.a: They are similar, but a bunion forms at the big toe and a tailor's bunion forms at the little toe.

title: Tailor's Bunion (Bunionette)

short: hammertoes, mallet toes, claw toes, and curly toes
lead: These are toe shapes where one or more small toes bend in an unusual way. A hammertoe bends at the middle joint, a mallet toe bends at the tip, and a claw toe curls at both joints. Curly toes tilt or curl under the neighboring toe.
They can start in childhood or appear later in life. Catching the bend while the toe is still flexible gives you more choices.
feels: A toe that stays bent or curled
Corns or calluses on top of the toe or at the tip
Pain or rubbing inside your shoes
Stiffness when you try to straighten the toe
causes: Muscle imbalance around the toe joints
Shoes that are too short or tight
Nerve conditions or arthritis
A family history of curled toes
diagnose: We check whether the toe still bends back into place or has become stiff. We also look for corns, sores, and nerve or muscle problems that may play a part. Weight-bearing X-rays show the joint position and any arthritis.
treat: Shoes with a deep, wide toe box give the toes room. Padding and toe sleeves can lower friction, and a podiatrist can trim corns safely in the office. Custom orthotics may help balance the pull on the toes. Simple stretching, and sometimes taping, can help a flexible toe stay straighter.
more: When a toe is rigid or keeps causing sores, a small procedure can release a tight tendon or straighten the joint. Your surgeon will match the method to how stiff the toe is.
recovery: Flexible toes may improve over several weeks with better shoes and stretching. After surgery, swelling can last a few months, and most people return to regular shoes in about six to twelve weeks.
when: Book a visit if a toe hurts, blisters, or has an open sore. Do not wait if you have diabetes, since small rubs can turn into serious wounds.

faqs.q: Can I straighten my toe with exercises alone?
faqs.a: If the toe is still flexible, exercises and good shoes can help. A stiff toe usually does not straighten without other care.

faqs.q: Why does the same toe keep forming a corn?
faqs.a: The bent toe rubs the shoe in the same spot again and again. Easing that pressure is the key to stopping it.

title: Hammertoes, Mallet Toes, Claw Toes & Curly Toes

short: overlapping toes, underlapping toes, and toe joint contractures
lead: Sometimes a toe rides up over its neighbor or tucks underneath it. A joint contracture means a toe joint has tightened and cannot move fully. These problems change how the toes line up and how shoes fit.
They may be present from birth or develop over time. Gentle care works best while the joint can still move.
feels: A toe sitting on top of or under the next toe
A joint that will not straighten or bend
Rubbing, blisters, or corns between the toes
Toe pain in closed shoes
causes: Tight tendons or ligaments in the toe
A toe shape present from birth
Pressure from bunions or crowded shoes
Nerve or muscle problems that pull the toe off line
diagnose: We move each toe gently to see how far it bends and whether it can be guided back into place. We check the skin for friction sores. X-rays show how the bones and joints line up.
treat: Toe spacers, splints, and taping can guide the toe into a better position. Soft padding protects the areas that rub. Stretching exercises help keep tight joints moving. Roomy shoes and orthotics can also reduce crowding.
more: If the joint has become fixed or sores keep returning, surgery can lengthen tight tissue or realign the toe. Many mild cases do not need an operation.
recovery: Improvement with taping and stretching is usually gradual and may take weeks to months. Results depend on how stiff the toe was at the start.
when: Come in if the toe is painful, if the skin breaks down, or if the position is getting worse. Children with an overlapping toe are best seen early, since treatment can work better while young.

faqs.q: Does my child need treatment for an overlapping toe?
faqs.a: Some children get help from gentle taping or splinting. A podiatrist can tell you whether it is worth trying based on how flexible the toe is.

faqs.q: Can a tight joint loosen up?
faqs.a: Mild tightness may ease with regular stretching. A joint that is truly fixed may need a procedure.

title: Overlapping, Underlapping & Joint Contractures

lead: Ball-of-foot pain is soreness under the front of your foot, just behind the toes. Metatarsalgia is the name for this pain when the long foot bones (metatarsals) take too much pressure. It often feels like a bruise.
People who run, stand all day, or wear thin-soled or high-heeled shoes notice it most. Finding the cause early can stop the pain from spreading to other parts of the foot.
feels: Aching or burning under the ball of the foot
A feeling like a pebble under your toes
Pain that grows with walking or standing
Relief when you rest with your shoes off
causes: High heels or shoes with thin soles
Running or jumping sports with heavy impact
Foot shapes with a high arch or long metatarsal bones
Extra body weight or a tight calf muscle
diagnose: We ask about your shoes and daily activity, then press along the forefoot to find the sore spot. We also watch you stand and walk. X-rays can show bone length and stress injuries, and ultrasound or MRI may be used when we suspect soft tissue damage.
treat: Cushioned shoes with a rocker sole can spread pressure across the foot. Metatarsal pads and custom orthotics move load away from the sore area. Rest from high-impact activity, ice, and calf stretching are often helpful. Physical therapy and, at times, an injection may calm stubborn pain.
more: Surgery is rarely needed. When other care fails, a procedure may adjust a metatarsal bone or release a tight calf muscle to reduce forefoot pressure.
recovery: Many people feel real relief in four to eight weeks once pressure is offloaded. Longer recovery is possible if another problem is also present.
when: See a podiatrist if pain lasts more than a couple of weeks or if it changes how you walk. Seek care sooner if you notice swelling, numbness, or a toe drifting out of place.

faqs.q: Is ball-of-foot pain the same as a stress fracture?
faqs.a: No, but they can feel alike. An exam and imaging help tell them apart.

faqs.q: Can I keep running with this pain?
faqs.a: Often you can cut back and change shoes or inserts while healing. Ask us for a plan that fits your sport.

title: Ball-of-Foot Pain, Metatarsalgia & Forefoot Overload

lead: The plantar plate is a strong band of tissue under the joint at the base of each toe. It holds the toe in place and helps it push off the ground. Capsulitis is swelling of the joint lining around it, and a tear means the band has been stretched or torn.
Most often it affects the second toe joint. Early care can protect the joint before the toe starts to drift.
feels: Pain under the ball of the foot at the base of a toe
Swelling at the joint
A toe that starts to float up or drift sideways
A feeling of walking on a folded sock
causes: Repeated stress on the forefoot from activity
A long second toe or a bunion pushing on the joint
Tight calf muscles that overload the front of the foot
Steroid injections or an old injury near the joint
diagnose: We test the joint by gently moving the toe to see if it feels loose or unstable. Ultrasound or MRI can show the plantar plate and whether it is inflamed or torn. X-rays help us check the bones.
treat: Taping the toe to hold it in a better position takes strain off the plate. A stiff-soled or rocker shoe, a metatarsal pad, and orthotics reduce load on the joint. Some patients wear a walking boot for a short time. Physical therapy and shockwave therapy may be added for lingering pain.
more: If the tear is large or the toe keeps drifting, surgery can repair the plate and realign the toe. Early cases often improve without it.
recovery: Healing is slow, and many people need eight to twelve weeks or longer to feel much better. Surgical recovery can take several months.
when: See us if pain at the base of a toe lasts beyond a couple of weeks or if the toe begins to shift. Treating early gives the best chance of avoiding surgery.

faqs.q: Why is my second toe moving away from the big toe?
faqs.a: A weakened plantar plate can let the toe drift. This is a sign to be checked soon.

faqs.q: Are cortisone shots a good idea here?
faqs.a: They can help some joint pain but may weaken the tissue if overused. We weigh the risks with you first.

title: Capsulitis & Plantar Plate Injuries and Tears

lead: Morton's neuroma is a thickening of the tissue around a nerve between the toe bones. It usually occurs between the third and fourth toes. The pinched nerve can cause sharp, odd sensations in the front of the foot.
It is more common in adults, and women notice it more often. Acting early may help you avoid long-term nerve irritation.
feels: Burning or tingling in the ball of the foot and toes
A feeling of a lump or wrinkled sock under the toes
Sharp pain that eases when you take off your shoes
Numbness in the space between two toes
causes: Tight or narrow shoes that squeeze the toes
High heels that shift weight onto the forefoot
Repeated pressure from running or court sports
A flat foot or other foot shape that stresses the nerve
diagnose: We press on the space between the toes and squeeze the forefoot to see if it brings on your symptoms. Ultrasound can often show the thickened nerve, and MRI may be used if the picture is unclear. X-rays help rule out other causes such as a stress fracture.
treat: Wide shoes with a low heel give the nerve room. A small pad placed behind the ball of the foot can spread the toes apart, and custom orthotics can reduce pinching. Ice and rest from aggravating activity may calm flare-ups. An injection near the nerve is sometimes used for stubborn pain.
more: If symptoms continue after good non-surgical care, surgery can release pressure on the nerve or remove the affected piece of it. Your surgeon will explain the tradeoffs, including some lasting numbness.
recovery: Many people improve over several weeks to a few months with shoe changes and pads. After surgery, expect a few weeks in protective footwear and gradual return to activity.
when: Make a visit if burning or numbness in your toes lasts more than a week or two. Do not wait if the pain wakes you at night or keeps you from doing daily tasks.

faqs.q: Is a neuroma a tumor?
faqs.a: No. It is a thickening of tissue around a nerve, not a cancer.

faqs.q: Can I still wear heels?
faqs.a: Heels tend to make it worse. Save them for short events and choose roomy, low shoes most of the time.

title: Morton's Neuroma (Intermetatarsal Neuroma)

short: Freiberg's disease and intractable plantar keratosis
lead: Freiberg's disease happens when the head of a metatarsal bone, most often the second, loses blood supply and collapses a little. Intractable plantar keratosis (IPK) is a deep, painful callus under the ball of the foot that keeps coming back. Both cause pain when the front of the foot takes weight.
Freiberg's is seen mostly in teens and young women. IPK can affect many adults. Care often begins with simple pressure relief.
feels: Deep, aching pain at the base of a toe
Swelling and stiffness in the toe joint
A hard, painful spot under the ball of the foot
Pain that returns even after the callus is trimmed
causes: Repeated stress on a metatarsal bone during growth
A long metatarsal that carries extra load
A bone that sits lower than its neighbors
Past injury to the forefoot
diagnose: We examine the sore area and trim any callus to see what is underneath. X-rays can show flattening of the bone in Freiberg's disease or a low bone head in IPK. MRI may be used to check bone health in early Freiberg's.
treat: Offloading is the main goal. A stiff-soled shoe, a walking boot for a short time, and custom orthotics with padding around the sore area can lower pressure. For IPK, we can safely shave the callus in the office to ease pain. Rest from high-impact sports helps Freiberg's settle.
more: When pain continues, surgery can smooth the bone, remove damaged joint surface, or shift the bone to relieve pressure. The choice depends on the age of the patient and the condition of the joint.
recovery: Many people feel better after a few months of offloading, though the joint may stay a bit stiff. Recovery after surgery is often two to four months.
when: Come in if forefoot pain lasts more than a few weeks, especially in a teen. Also see us if a callus keeps coming back or hurts to walk on.

faqs.q: Why does my callus keep returning?
faqs.a: A callus grows back when the same spot keeps taking too much pressure. Padding and orthotics aim to fix the cause, not just the skin.

faqs.q: Is Freiberg's disease permanent?
faqs.a: The bone changes may stay, but pain can often be controlled with care.

title: Freiberg's Disease & Intractable Plantar Keratosis (IPK)

lead: Flat feet means the arch of the foot is low or touches the ground when you stand. Acquired flatfoot is when the arch falls later in life, often because a supporting tendon weakens. Many people with flat feet have no trouble at all.
When pain does show up, it is often along the inside of the foot or ankle. A new change in your arch is worth having checked.
feels: Tired, achy feet after standing or walking
Pain along the inside of the ankle or arch
Swelling on the inner ankle
Feet that seem to turn outward
causes: Weakening of the tendon that lifts the arch
Foot shape passed down in families
Injury, arthritis, or extra body weight
Aging and wear over many years
diagnose: We watch you stand, walk, and rise up on your toes to see how the arch works. A standing X-ray of the foot and ankle shows the bone alignment. Ultrasound or MRI may be added if a tendon injury is suspected.
treat: Supportive shoes and custom orthotics are the mainstay for a painful flat foot. A brace or walking boot can rest an irritated tendon. Physical therapy builds strength in the foot and calf. Weight management, ice, and activity changes also help.
more: Surgery is reserved for people with ongoing pain or a worsening shape despite other care. Options include repairing tendons, realigning bones, or fusing painful joints.
recovery: With good support, many people feel better in a matter of weeks to a few months. Surgical recovery is longer and may take several months.
when: See a podiatrist if your arch has changed, or if the inside of your ankle hurts or swells. Get checked promptly if one foot looks flatter than the other.

faqs.q: Do all flat feet need treatment?
faqs.a: No. If your feet do not hurt and you move well, you may not need any care.

faqs.q: Can flat feet cause knee or back pain?
faqs.a: They may add strain higher up in some people. Supportive inserts can sometimes help.

title: Flat Feet (Pes Planus) in Adults, Including Acquired Flatfoot
parentTitle: Flat Feet, High Arches & Alignment Disorders

lead: Progressive collapsing foot deformity, or PCFD, is a slow change in the foot and ankle where the arch sinks and the heel and foot shift out of line. It used to be called adult acquired flatfoot. It often begins with a worn-out tendon on the inner ankle.
It tends to appear in middle age and can worsen over time. Catching it early helps protect the joints from wear.
feels: Pain and swelling along the inner ankle
An arch that slowly gets lower
A heel that tilts outward
Trouble standing on your toes or walking far
causes: Long-term strain on the posterior tibial tendon
Ligament weakness along the inside of the ankle
Obesity, diabetes, or high blood pressure
Past injury or inflammatory joint disease
diagnose: We check tendon strength, heel position, and how flexible the foot is. Standing X-rays show how far the bones have shifted, and MRI or ultrasound shows the state of the tendon. This tells us how advanced the problem is.
treat: Early care includes a custom orthotic, a supportive brace or boot, and sturdy shoes. Physical therapy works on strength and balance. Anti-inflammatory measures and rest can settle a flare. Taping or an injection may be used in selected cases.
more: When bracing does not control pain or the shape keeps changing, surgery may rebuild the arch, move tendons, or fuse joints. The plan depends on how stiff the foot has become.
recovery: Non-surgical care may take a few months to show its full effect. Surgical recovery often takes several months, with walking in stages.
when: See us as soon as you notice a falling arch or steady pain on the inner ankle. Early treatment gives you more options.

faqs.q: Will PCFD keep getting worse?
faqs.a: It can, but bracing and other care may slow the change. Checkups help us follow it.

faqs.q: Is it different from ordinary flat feet?
faqs.a: Yes. PCFD is a changing problem with tendon damage, while many flat feet are stable and painless.

title: Progressive Collapsing Foot Deformity (PCFD)
parentTitle: Flat Feet, High Arches & Alignment Disorders

lead: A high arch, or pes cavus, is a foot with an arch that stays raised even when you stand. A cavovarus foot also has a heel that tilts inward. The foot becomes stiff and puts extra load on the heel and ball.
Some people are born with it. In others, a nerve or muscle condition is behind it, so a careful exam matters.
feels: Pain in the ball or heel of the foot
Frequent ankle sprains or a wobbly ankle
Toes that curl or claw
Calluses on the heel, ball, or outer edge
causes: An inherited foot shape
Nerve and muscle conditions that pull the foot
Old injuries to the foot or ankle
Imbalance between strong and weak leg muscles
diagnose: We look at your arch, heel angle, and toe position, and test strength and feeling in your legs. Standing X-rays show alignment. We may suggest nerve or MRI testing if we suspect a hidden cause.
treat: Cushioned shoes with a wide sole absorb shock. Custom orthotics spread pressure across the foot rather than only the heel and ball. An ankle brace can add stability if you often roll your ankle. Physical therapy and calf stretching also help.
more: When pain or ankle instability continues, surgery can rebalance tendons, correct the heel position, or reshape bones. Many people do well without an operation.
recovery: Better shoes and orthotics often bring relief within a few weeks. Surgical recovery may take three to six months or more.
when: Book a visit if you sprain your ankle often or have foot pain that lasts. Also come in if you notice new weakness, numbness, or a change in your arch.

faqs.q: Why do I keep spraining my ankle?
faqs.a: A high arch shifts weight to the outer foot, which makes rolling the ankle easier. A brace and strength work can help.

faqs.q: Can a high arch come from a nerve problem?
faqs.a: Yes, sometimes. That is why we check strength and feeling along with the foot.

title: High Arches (Pes Cavus) & Cavovarus Foot
parentTitle: Flat Feet, High Arches & Alignment Disorders

lead: An accessory navicular is an extra piece of bone or cartilage on the inner side of the foot, next to the main navicular bone. It is present from birth in some people. It becomes a problem, called a syndrome, when it gets irritated and painful.
Symptoms often start in the teen years or after a twist or sports injury. Early care can help calm the area before the pain becomes a habit.
feels: A bony bump on the inside of the midfoot
Redness or tenderness over the bump
Pain in the arch with activity
Soreness from shoes rubbing the bump
causes: An extra bone present from birth
Rubbing from shoes or straps
Overuse in sports or long walks
A flat foot that pulls on the tendon attached to the bone
diagnose: We press on the bump and check the tendon on the inner foot for pain or weakness. A foot X-ray shows the extra bone clearly. MRI or ultrasound can show swelling around it if the cause is uncertain.
treat: Rest and ice can settle a flare. Padding and shoes that do not press on the bump reduce irritation, and arch supports can ease the pull on the tendon. A short time in a boot or cast helps some sore feet. Physical therapy may be added as pain improves.
more: If pain stays despite these steps, surgery can remove the extra bone and reattach the tendon. Many people never need it.
recovery: Most people improve over several weeks to a couple of months with rest and support. After surgery, expect walking in a boot at first and a return to sports in about three months, though this varies.
when: See a podiatrist if a bump on the inner foot is painful or keeps returning. Bring your teen in if arch pain is limiting sports or school.

faqs.q: Is the extra bone dangerous?
faqs.a: No. Many people have one and never know it. It only needs care if it hurts.

faqs.q: Will my child outgrow it?
faqs.a: The bone does not go away, but symptoms often ease with care and growth.

title: Accessory Navicular Syndrome
parentTitle: Flat Feet, High Arches & Alignment Disorders

short: foot and ankle malalignment and leg-length differences
lead: Malalignment means the bones of the foot, ankle, or leg do not line up as they should. A leg-length difference means one leg is shorter than the other. Either one can change the way your body carries weight.
Small differences are common and often cause no trouble. Larger ones can lead to pain in the feet, knees, hips, or back.
feels: Uneven wear on the soles of your shoes
Pain in the foot, knee, hip, or low back
A limp or a tilt when you walk
Ankles that roll in or out
causes: Growth differences between the legs
A past fracture or surgery
Arthritis or joint wear
Flat feet, high arches, or tight muscles
diagnose: We check how you stand, measure both legs, and look at joint position while you walk. Standing X-rays of the feet and ankles help us see the true alignment. Longer leg X-rays may be arranged to measure length.
treat: A small shoe lift can even out a modest leg-length difference. Custom orthotics correct foot position and share pressure more evenly. Physical therapy works on strength and flexibility, and supportive shoes help you stay steady. Bracing may add support around the ankle.
more: Surgery is not common. It may be considered for a painful bone deformity or a large difference that other care cannot manage.
recovery: Lifts and orthotics often help within a few weeks, though your body needs time to adjust. Progress depends on the cause and how large the difference is.
when: See us if you notice uneven shoe wear, lasting pain, or a limp that will not go away. Children with an uneven walk should be checked early.

faqs.q: How much leg-length difference matters?
faqs.a: It depends on the person. A small difference may not cause trouble, so we treat based on symptoms and exam.

faqs.q: Can a shoe lift fix it?
faqs.a: For many mild cases, a lift eases strain. It does not change the bones.

title: Foot & Ankle Malalignment and Leg-Length Discrepancy
parentTitle: Flat Feet, High Arches & Alignment Disorders

lead: Pronation is the normal inward roll of the foot as you step. Overpronation means the foot rolls in too far. Supination, or underpronation, means the foot rolls too little and stays on the outer edge.
Both can change how force travels through your feet and legs. Runners and active people often notice them first.
feels: Sore arches or heels after activity
Shin, knee, or hip aches
Shoes that wear down on one side
Frequent ankle rolling or shin splints
causes: Flat or high arch shapes
Tight calf muscles or weak foot muscles
Worn-out or poorly fitting shoes
Running on hard or uneven surfaces
diagnose: We watch how your foot lands and pushes off while you stand and walk. We look at your shoes for wear patterns. X-rays are used if we suspect a bone problem behind the pain.
treat: Shoes matched to your foot type make a large difference. Custom orthotics guide the foot toward a steadier motion. Calf stretches and foot strengthening build support, and physical therapy can help with running form. Ice and rest calm overworked tissues.
more: Surgery is rarely needed for pronation problems. It is only considered when a structural issue such as a collapsing arch is causing steady pain.
recovery: Many people feel better in a few weeks after changing shoes and adding inserts. Full comfort may take a few months as your body adapts.
when: See a podiatrist if pain keeps returning or if you have repeated injuries. Come in sooner if pain limits your usual activity.

faqs.q: How do I know my foot type?
faqs.a: Wear patterns on your shoes offer clues, but an exam gives a more reliable answer.

faqs.q: Do I need custom orthotics or store-bought inserts?
faqs.a: Some people do well with store-bought ones. Custom devices are made for your foot and may help when those fall short.

title: Overpronation & Supination
parentTitle: Flat Feet, High Arches & Alignment Disorders

lead: Gait is the way you walk. A gait problem means your steps look or feel different from usual, such as limping, dragging a foot, or turning the feet in or out. The cause may be in the foot, but it can also come from the leg, hip, back, or nerves.
Changes in walking can raise the chance of falls and pain. Looking into the cause early can help you stay active and steady.
feels: Limping or favoring one foot
Toes that catch or drag on the ground
Feeling unsteady or off balance
Foot, knee, or hip pain after walking
causes: Foot pain, arthritis, or deformity
Weak muscles or nerve problems
Differences in leg length
Old injuries, or being in a cast or brace
diagnose: We watch you walk, stand, and turn, and we look at the shape and strength of your feet and legs. X-rays can show bone or joint problems, and MRI or ultrasound may be used for soft tissue. If we suspect a nerve or other medical cause, we may refer you for more testing.
treat: Treatment depends on the cause. Custom orthotics, braces, and supportive shoes can improve how your foot moves. Physical therapy builds strength and balance. Treating foot pain or sores at the source often helps your walking as well.
more: If a deformity or joint problem is behind the gait change, surgery may be an option to relieve pain and improve motion. Many people improve with non-surgical care.
recovery: Some people notice better steps within a few weeks of new shoes or inserts. Others need a few months, especially if strength or nerve issues are involved.
when: See a podiatrist if your walking changes without a clear reason or if you trip or fall more often. Seek urgent care if a sudden change comes with weakness, numbness, or trouble speaking.

faqs.q: Can foot problems really change how I walk?
faqs.a: Yes. Pain or stiffness makes you shift your steps, which can strain other joints.

faqs.q: Should I use a cane or brace?
faqs.a: Sometimes they help. We can advise what suits your needs and how to use them safely.

title: Gait & Walking Abnormalities
parentTitle: Flat Feet, High Arches & Alignment Disorders

short: chronic ankle pain and ankle instability
lead: Chronic ankle instability means the ankle keeps giving way. It often follows a sprain that never fully healed, leaving the ligaments loose and the ankle less steady. Pain can come and go, or stay for months.
It is common in athletes, but anyone who has sprained an ankle more than once can develop it. Getting care early can protect the joint from more damage.
feels: The ankle rolls or gives way on uneven ground
Ongoing aching on the outer side of the ankle
Swelling that returns after activity
A feeling that the ankle cannot be trusted
causes: Past sprains that healed poorly
Ligaments stretched or torn and never tightened
Weak muscles around the ankle
Rehab stopped too early after an injury
diagnose: We ask how the ankle has been giving way and test how loose it feels. X-rays check the bones and joint alignment. If we suspect damage to ligaments, tendons, or cartilage, we may order an MRI or ultrasound.
treat: Most people start with physical therapy to build strength and balance. A brace or taping can steady the ankle during sports and hard work. Shoes with good support also help. Some people benefit from an injection to calm irritated tissue in the joint.
more: If the ankle still gives way after a good try at care, surgery can tighten or repair the ligaments. Any other damage found inside the joint can often be treated at the same time.
recovery: Non-surgical care often takes several weeks to a few months of steady work. After surgery, full return to sports can take about four to six months or longer.
when: See a podiatrist if your ankle has given way more than once or aches for weeks. Get seen soon if it swells, locks, or you cannot trust it to hold your weight.

faqs.q: Will a brace fix my unstable ankle?
faqs.a: A brace can add support and lower the risk of rolling. It works best together with strengthening and balance exercises.

faqs.q: Can I keep exercising with an unstable ankle?
faqs.a: Low-impact activity is often fine, but twisting sports may be risky. Ask us what is safe for you.

title: Ankle Pain & Chronic Ankle Instability

lead: An ankle sprain is an injury to the ligaments, the strong bands that hold the ankle bones together. Most sprains happen on the outer side. A high ankle sprain affects the ligaments just above the joint, between the two leg bones.
Sprains happen when you twist or roll the foot, often in sports or on uneven ground. Proper care early helps the ligaments heal and lowers the chance of another sprain.
feels: Pain and swelling around the ankle after a twist
Bruising on the side or top of the foot
Trouble putting full weight on the foot
Pain above the ankle when the foot turns outward
causes: Rolling the foot on a curb or uneven ground
Landing awkwardly after a jump
A twisting force while the foot is planted
Weak ankles or a past sprain
diagnose: We check where it hurts, how much swelling there is, and how stable the ankle feels. X-rays help rule out a broken bone. A high ankle sprain may need special stress views or an MRI to see the ligaments above the joint.
treat: Early care includes rest, ice, gentle compression, and keeping the foot raised. We may use a brace or boot to protect the ankle, and crutches if walking hurts. Once pain settles, physical therapy restores motion, strength, and balance. High ankle sprains often need a longer time of protection.
more: Surgery is not needed for most sprains. It may be considered for a high ankle sprain that makes the leg bones spread apart, or when the ankle stays loose after care.
recovery: A mild sprain may feel better in two to six weeks. Moderate or high ankle sprains can take two to three months or more.
when: See a podiatrist if you cannot walk on the foot, the ankle looks out of shape, or swelling and bruising are large. Also come in if pain is not improving after a few days.

faqs.q: How do I know if it is a sprain or a break?
faqs.a: Both can cause swelling and pain, so it is hard to tell at home. An X-ray gives a clear answer.

faqs.q: Why does a high ankle sprain take longer to heal?
faqs.a: The ligaments above the ankle handle a lot of stress with every step. They need more time to settle.

title: Ankle Sprains (Lateral and High / Syndesmotic)

short: ankle ligament tears and joint impingement
lead: A ligament tear means one or more of the bands around the ankle have ripped, partly or fully. Impingement is different. It happens when soft tissue or bone gets pinched at the front or back of the ankle as it moves.
These problems often follow a bad sprain or repeated ankle stress. Dancers and runners are often affected. Finding the cause early can keep small problems from becoming lasting ones.
feels: Sharp pinching pain when the ankle bends
Swelling that lingers after an injury
A catching feeling deep in the joint
Pain when pushing off or squatting
causes: A severe sprain or repeated sprains
Extra bone growth at the joint edge
Scar tissue after an ankle injury
Repeated deep bending, as in dance or sport
diagnose: We press on the ankle and move it to find which tissue is pinched or torn. X-rays can show bone spurs. An MRI or ultrasound shows ligaments and soft tissue in more detail.
treat: Rest and a brace or boot can calm the ankle at first. Physical therapy rebuilds strength and steadier movement. Shoe changes, taping, and activity changes can lower stress on the joint. An injection may ease pain and swelling from pinched tissue.
more: If pain stays despite good care, surgery can repair torn ligaments or clean out scar tissue and bone spurs. Many of these procedures use small cuts.
recovery: Non-surgical recovery often takes six to twelve weeks. After surgery, expect a few months before returning to full activity.
when: See a podiatrist if ankle pain or swelling lasts more than a couple of weeks after an injury. Come sooner if the ankle catches, locks, or feels loose.

faqs.q: Can a torn ligament heal on its own?
faqs.a: Some partial tears heal well with a brace and therapy. Complete tears may stay loose and need further care.

faqs.q: What does impingement feel like?
faqs.a: Most people feel a pinch at the front or back of the ankle when it bends far. It often eases with rest.

title: Ankle Ligament Tears & Joint Impingement

short: ankle synovitis and osteochondral lesions of the talus
lead: Synovitis is swelling of the thin lining inside the ankle joint. An osteochondral lesion is damage to the cartilage and the bone under it on the talus, the bone that sits at the top of the foot.
Both can follow an ankle sprain or fracture that seems to have healed. The ankle may still ache, swell, or feel stuck long afterward, so it is worth having it checked.
feels: Deep ankle pain that lasts after a sprain
Swelling inside the joint
Clicking, locking, or catching
Stiffness, especially after rest
causes: A past sprain or ankle fracture
Repeated small injuries to the joint
Blood flow trouble to a small area of bone
Ongoing irritation of the joint lining
diagnose: X-rays may look normal, since cartilage damage can be hard to see. We often order an MRI or CT scan to view the talus and joint lining. We also compare your symptoms with your injury history.
treat: Early care may include a boot or brace to unload the joint, along with rest from impact. Anti-inflammatory approaches and injections can settle a swollen joint lining. Physical therapy helps keep the ankle moving and strong. Shoe support and activity changes protect the area while it heals.
more: If pain continues, surgery can clean out the lining, repair the damaged area, or stimulate new cartilage growth. The best option depends on the size and place of the lesion.
recovery: Mild cases may settle over several weeks to a few months. Larger lesions or surgery can mean six months or more before full activity.
when: See a podiatrist if ankle pain, swelling, or catching goes on for weeks after a sprain. A normal X-ray does not always mean the joint is fine.

faqs.q: Why did my ankle still hurt after the sprain healed?
faqs.a: Sometimes the joint lining or cartilage was hurt too. These problems can hide on plain X-rays.

faqs.q: Will I need surgery for a talus lesion?
faqs.a: Many small lesions improve without it. Surgery is usually kept for pain that does not respond to care.

title: Ankle Synovitis & Osteochondral Lesions of the Talus

lead: The posterior tibial tendon runs along the inside of the ankle and holds up your arch. When it is swollen, worn, or torn, the arch can slowly drop. This is called posterior tibial tendon dysfunction, or PTTD.
It is most common in adults, especially women over 40, but can affect others. Early treatment can slow the flattening of the foot and protect the tendon.
feels: Pain and swelling along the inside of the ankle
An arch that looks lower than before
Feet that turn outward as you walk
Trouble standing on your toes on one foot
causes: Overuse from walking, running, or standing a lot
A fall or twist that strains the tendon
Flat feet or a weak arch
Age-related wear, obesity, or diabetes
diagnose: We watch you stand and walk, and we look at your arch and heel from behind. We ask you to rise up on your toes to test tendon strength. X-rays show the arch shape and any joint changes, and an MRI or ultrasound can show swelling or tears.
treat: A boot or brace can rest the tendon in the early stage. Custom orthotics or braces then support the arch and lower strain. Supportive shoes and physical therapy help build strength and stability. Some people also use taping or an injection to calm pain.
more: If the tendon is badly torn or the foot keeps flattening, surgery can repair the tendon, move another tendon over, or realign bones. The choice depends on how stiff or flexible the foot is.
recovery: Early cases often improve in a few months with steady support. Surgery recovery can take six months to a year.
when: See a podiatrist if the inside of your ankle hurts and your arch seems to be falling. Do not wait, since early stages respond best.

faqs.q: Is a flat foot from PTTD the same as flat feet I was born with?
faqs.a: No. PTTD develops over time and causes pain, while some flat feet are lifelong and painless.

faqs.q: Can orthotics stop PTTD from getting worse?
faqs.a: They can lower strain on the tendon and slow the change. They work best with good shoes and follow-up.

title: Posterior Tibial Tendinitis & PTTD (Tendon Dysfunction and Tears)

lead: The peroneal tendons run down the outer side of the ankle. They help keep the ankle steady and turn the foot outward. They can become inflamed, worn, torn, or slip out of place.
Runners and people with high arches or unstable ankles often have these problems. Early care can prevent a small irritation from becoming a tear.
feels: Pain and swelling behind the outer ankle bone
A snapping or popping feeling on the outside
Weakness when turning the foot outward
Pain that grows with activity
causes: Repeated stress from running or jumping
Past ankle sprains
A high-arched foot that loads the outer ankle
A sudden twist that pushes the tendon out of place
diagnose: We feel along the tendons and test their strength. We may move your ankle to see if the tendon slips. Ultrasound can show the tendon moving, and an MRI shows tears and swelling.
treat: Rest, a brace, or a short time in a boot can calm the tendon. Physical therapy builds strength and balance. Orthotics or shoe changes can reduce pressure on the outer ankle. Ice and gentle stretching can also help settle pain.
more: When a tendon is torn or keeps slipping, surgery can repair it or deepen the groove where it sits. Choices depend on how much of the tendon is hurt.
recovery: Mild irritation may improve in four to twelve weeks. Surgery usually needs a few months of protected healing and therapy.
when: See a podiatrist if the outer ankle hurts and swells or you feel a snap. Come in soon after a sprain if the ankle still feels weak.

faqs.q: Why does my outer ankle snap?
faqs.a: The tendon may be slipping over the ankle bone. It is worth an exam to check for a tear.

faqs.q: Can peroneal tendon pain be mistaken for a sprain?
faqs.a: Yes, the two can feel much alike. A careful exam and imaging tell them apart.

title: Peroneal Tendinitis, Tendinosis, Tears & Subluxation

lead: Flexor tendons bend the toes and extensor tendons lift them. Either type can be strained, inflamed, cut, or torn. A full rupture means the tendon has snapped apart.
These injuries can come from overuse, cuts, or sudden force. Because toes and the front of the foot are needed for every step, early care matters.
feels: Pain or swelling along the top or bottom of the foot
Trouble lifting or curling a toe
A pop at the moment of injury
Weakness when pushing off or stepping
causes: Repeated stress from running or dancing
Cuts or deep wounds to the foot
Sudden force such as a hard landing
Tight shoes rubbing over the tendon
diagnose: We test how well each toe and the ankle move against resistance. We look for gaps or tenderness along the tendon. Ultrasound or MRI can confirm a tear, and X-rays check for bone injury.
treat: Mild strains often improve with rest, ice, and supportive shoes. Taping, a brace, or a boot can protect the tendon. Physical therapy restores motion and strength once pain allows. Injections are used with care and only in select cases.
more: A fully torn tendon often needs surgery to repair it or replace the missing part. Partial tears may heal without an operation.
recovery: Strains may take a few weeks to a couple of months. Repaired tendons often need protection and therapy for three months or more.
when: See a podiatrist right away after a cut, pop, or sudden loss of toe movement. Also come in if tendon pain lasts more than a couple of weeks.

faqs.q: Can a torn toe tendon heal without surgery?
faqs.a: Partial tears sometimes do. A complete tear usually needs repair to restore full movement.

faqs.q: Does it matter how soon I get care after a cut on my foot?
faqs.a: Yes. Early repair often gives better results and lowers the risk of infection.

title: Flexor & Extensor Tendon Injuries and Ruptures

short: foot and ankle bursitis, muscle strains, and soft tissue injuries
lead: Bursae are small fluid-filled cushions that help tissues glide over bone. When one is irritated, it swells and hurts, which is called bursitis. Muscle strains and other soft tissue injuries are overstretched or torn muscle fibers and supporting tissue.
These injuries are common in active people and in those who wear tight shoes. Most respond well when cared for early.
feels: A tender, puffy spot near a joint or heel
Pain when you press on or move the area
Muscle soreness, tightness, or cramping
Bruising after a sudden pull or twist
causes: Shoes that rub or press on one spot
Repeated activity without enough rest
A sudden stretch or awkward step
Direct bumps or pressure on the area
diagnose: We find the exact spot of pain and see how it responds to touch and movement. X-rays can rule out a bone problem. Ultrasound or MRI can show a swollen bursa or a torn muscle.
treat: Rest, ice, and shoes that avoid the sore area are often the first steps. Padding, taping, or orthotics can reduce pressure and strain. Gentle stretching and physical therapy help muscles recover. An injection can calm a stubborn swollen bursa.
more: Surgery is rarely needed for these injuries. It may be an option for a bursa that keeps coming back or a large muscle tear.
recovery: Many people feel better within two to six weeks. Larger strains or long-standing bursitis can take a few months.
when: See a podiatrist if a swollen spot is hot, red, or getting worse. Also come in if pain keeps you from normal activity for more than a week or two.

faqs.q: Is bursitis the same as an infection?
faqs.a: No, but a swollen bursa can sometimes become infected. Heat, redness, or fever means you should be seen quickly.

faqs.q: Should I stretch a pulled foot muscle right away?
faqs.a: Not at first. Let it rest, then add gentle movement as pain settles.

title: Foot & Ankle Bursitis, Muscle Strains & Soft-Tissue Injuries

short: osteoarthritis of the foot and ankle
lead: Osteoarthritis is the slow wearing down of the smooth cartilage that cushions a joint. In the foot and ankle it can affect the big toe, the midfoot, the ankle, or the subtalar joint under the ankle.
It is more common with age and after past injuries. The pain usually builds slowly, and early care can keep you walking comfortably.
feels: Aching and stiffness in the joint, worse after rest
Swelling or a bony bump over the joint
Pain with long walks or on hard floors
Less motion in the foot or ankle
causes: Years of normal wear on the joint
Old sprains, breaks, or joint injuries
Flat or high-arched foot shape
Family history of arthritis
diagnose: We check joint motion, swelling, and how you walk. Weight-bearing X-rays show narrowed joint space and bone spurs. An MRI or CT scan may help plan care if the picture is not clear.
treat: Supportive shoes with a stiff sole can take stress off the joint. Custom orthotics, braces, and sometimes a rocker-bottom shoe help you move with less pain. Physical therapy keeps nearby muscles strong. Injections may calm flare-ups for a time.
more: When pain limits daily life despite other care, surgery can clean up the joint, fuse it, or in some ankles replace it. Your surgeon will match the option to the joint and your goals.
recovery: Non-surgical care often brings steady relief over several weeks, though arthritis is ongoing. Surgery recovery is often three to six months, sometimes longer.
when: See a podiatrist if joint pain or stiffness lasts more than a few weeks or limits your walking. Come sooner if a joint becomes hot, red, and swollen.

faqs.q: Can I still exercise with foot arthritis?
faqs.a: Yes, low-impact choices like cycling or swimming are usually gentler on the joints.

faqs.q: Does arthritis always get worse?
faqs.a: It often progresses slowly, but good shoes and support can reduce symptoms for many years.

title: Osteoarthritis of the Foot, Ankle, Midfoot & Subtalar Joint

lead: Post-traumatic arthritis is joint wear that starts after an injury such as a fracture, a bad sprain, or a dislocation. The injury harms the cartilage or changes how the joint lines up.
It can show up months or even years after the event. Ankles, heels, and midfoot joints are often affected, so a checkup is wise if pain lingers after an old injury.
feels: Pain in a joint you hurt in the past
Stiffness after sitting or in the morning
Swelling after being on your feet
A grinding or catching feeling
causes: A past broken bone that reached the joint
A dislocation or severe sprain
Bones that healed slightly out of line
Damage to cartilage at the time of injury
