diagnose: We ask about earlier injuries and look at how the joint moves. Weight-bearing X-rays show joint space loss and how the bones lined up. CT or MRI can add detail about cartilage and bone.
treat: Shoes with good cushioning and a firm sole help take load off the joint. Braces, orthotics, and activity changes can lessen daily pain. Physical therapy keeps the surrounding muscles strong. Injections may give relief during flare-ups.
more: If pain remains severe, surgery may include cleaning the joint, joining the bones (fusion), or an ankle replacement in selected cases. Choices depend on which joint is damaged and how you use your foot.
recovery: Many people manage symptoms well with non-surgical care over a few weeks to months. Surgical recovery often takes several months.
when: See a podiatrist if a past injury site keeps hurting or swelling. Early checks can guide care before the joint stiffens further.

faqs.q: Why is my old ankle break hurting years later?
faqs.a: Injuries can wear the cartilage over time, even after the bone has healed. Arthritis is a common reason.

faqs.q: Can this type of arthritis be prevented?
faqs.a: Not always. Getting good care after a joint injury may lower the risk.

title: Post-Traumatic Arthritis

short: rheumatoid and psoriatic arthritis of the foot and ankle
lead: Rheumatoid and psoriatic arthritis are conditions where the immune system attacks the joints. They often affect both feet and can also hit the ankles and toes.
Symptoms may flare and calm down. Because these diseases can harm joints if left alone, working with a podiatrist and a rheumatologist is important.
feels: Swelling and warmth in several joints
Morning stiffness that lasts a while
Toes that look swollen like sausages
Pain in both feet, often on both sides
causes: The immune system attacking joint lining
Family history of autoimmune disease
Psoriasis affecting the skin or nails
Triggers that are not fully understood
diagnose: We look at joint swelling, toe shape, and nail or skin changes. X-rays can show joint damage. Blood tests may help point toward an autoimmune cause, and ultrasound can show inflamed joint lining. We coordinate with your other doctors on the diagnosis.
treat: Medicines for the disease itself come from your rheumatology team. We help with foot comfort using roomy shoes, cushioned insoles, and custom orthotics. Padding and braces can protect painful joints. Physical therapy helps keep motion, and injections may calm a very swollen joint.
more: If joints become badly damaged or deformed, surgery may realign toes or fuse painful joints. It is used when other care no longer helps enough.
recovery: Foot symptoms often improve as the disease is controlled, which can take weeks to months. Surgery recovery varies, often several months.
when: See a podiatrist if you have swollen, stiff joints in both feet or toes that change shape. Do not wait, since early treatment can protect the joints.

faqs.q: Can foot care replace my arthritis medicine?
faqs.a: No. Foot care eases pain and protects joints, but disease treatment comes from your rheumatology team.

faqs.q: Why do my toes look swollen all over?
faqs.a: Psoriatic arthritis can inflame the whole toe. It is a known sign and worth mentioning to your doctors.

title: Rheumatoid & Psoriatic Arthritis of the Foot & Ankle

lead: Gout and pseudogout happen when tiny crystals build up in a joint and cause sudden swelling and pain. Gout is linked to uric acid crystals and often hits the big toe. Pseudogout involves a different crystal and often affects the ankle or midfoot.
An attack can come on fast, often overnight. Prompt care eases pain and helps prevent repeat attacks and joint damage.
feels: Sudden severe pain in one joint
Red, hot, swollen skin over the joint
A toe or ankle too tender to touch
Pain that peaks within hours
causes: High uric acid levels in the blood
Certain foods and drinks, especially alcohol
Some health conditions and medicines
Age and family history
diagnose: We look at the joint and ask about past attacks. Blood tests can check uric acid levels, though they may be normal during an attack. Fluid from the joint can show which crystals are present. X-rays or ultrasound may show crystal buildup or joint damage.
treat: Resting and raising the foot helps during an attack. Medicines to calm the flare are usually guided by your doctor. Changes in diet and fluids may lower the chance of repeat attacks. Comfortable, roomy shoes protect the joint while it settles.
more: Surgery is rarely needed. It may be used to remove large crystal deposits or repair a joint damaged by repeated attacks.
recovery: A flare often eases in several days to two weeks with care. Long-term control of the cause may take months.
when: See a podiatrist quickly if a joint suddenly becomes hot, red, and very painful. Seek urgent care if you also have a fever.

faqs.q: Is gout only in the big toe?
faqs.a: No. It often starts there but can affect the ankle, knee, or other joints.

faqs.q: Can foods really trigger gout?
faqs.a: Some can raise uric acid in certain people. A balanced diet and steady fluids help, and your doctor can guide you.

title: Gout & Pseudogout

short: foot and ankle joint stiffness and synovitis
lead: Joint stiffness means a joint feels tight and does not move as far as it should. Synovitis is swelling of the joint lining, which often causes the stiffness and pain.
It can follow an injury, overuse, or arthritis. Working on it early can help you keep normal movement in daily life.
feels: A tight, hard-to-move joint
Puffiness around the ankle or toe joint
Aching that eases as you warm up
Pain when moving the joint to its limit
causes: Irritation after an injury or surgery
Overuse of the joint
Arthritis in the joint
Long time in a cast or boot without motion
diagnose: We measure how far each joint moves and check for warmth and swelling. X-rays look for arthritis or bone changes. Ultrasound or MRI can show inflamed lining, and blood tests may be used if an inflammatory disease is suspected.
treat: Gentle stretching and warm-up movement help loosen the joint. Physical therapy guides safe strengthening and motion. Supportive shoes and orthotics lower strain. An injection may quiet a joint that stays swollen. Ice can help after activity.
more: If stiffness or swelling continues, minor procedures or surgery can remove inflamed lining or free up scar tissue. These steps are considered after other care has been tried.
recovery: Many joints loosen up over four to twelve weeks of steady work. Chronic causes like arthritis may need ongoing care.
when: See a podiatrist if a joint stays stiff or swollen for more than a couple of weeks. Come sooner if it is hot, red, or comes with fever.

faqs.q: Should I rest a stiff joint or keep moving it?
faqs.a: Gentle movement usually helps, while rest alone can make it stiffer. We can show you safe exercises.

faqs.q: Why is my ankle stiff after a cast?
faqs.a: Joints and muscles tighten when they are not used. Therapy usually helps restore motion.

title: Joint Stiffness & Synovitis

lead: A bone spur is a small extra growth of bone, often near a joint or where tendons pull. An osteochondral defect is a damaged spot in the joint's cartilage and the bone beneath it.
Many spurs cause no trouble, but some rub on tissue or limit motion. Defects can cause deep joint pain, so a clear diagnosis helps guide care.
feels: A hard bump you can feel or see
Pain when a shoe presses on the area
Deep joint ache with activity
Limited motion or a catching feeling
causes: Long-term stress or friction on the bone
Arthritis in the joint
Past injuries to the joint surface
Tight or poorly fitting shoes
diagnose: X-rays show most bone spurs clearly. For a defect in cartilage and bone, we often use an MRI or CT scan. We also check how your joint moves and where it hurts.
treat: Shoes with a roomy toe box or extra padding can take pressure off a spur. Orthotics, taping, and activity changes ease stress on the area. Physical therapy helps with joint motion and strength. Injections may calm painful, swollen tissue. Defects may need a boot or protected weight-bearing to heal.
more: A painful spur can be removed with surgery. Defects can be cleaned out, repaired, or encouraged to regrow cartilage, depending on their size.
recovery: Simple spur pain often eases in a few weeks with shoe changes. Surgery for a spur or defect may take two to six months for full recovery.
when: See a podiatrist if a bump keeps hurting or a joint aches deeply for weeks. Also come in if pain is changing how you walk.

faqs.q: Do bone spurs need to be removed?
faqs.a: Most do not. They are treated only if they cause ongoing pain or limit movement.

faqs.q: Will a spur grow back after surgery?
faqs.a: It can in some cases, especially if the cause remains. Good shoes and follow-up lower the chance.

title: Bone Spurs & Osteochondral Defects

lead: A fracture is a break in a bone. In the foot and ankle, this can be a small crack or a bone that has moved out of place. Common spots include the fifth metatarsal, the Jones area, the heel bone, the talus, and the navicular.

These breaks often follow a fall, a twist, a car crash, or a heavy object landing on the foot. Most people notice pain and swelling right away. Early care helps the bone line up and heal in a good position.
feels: Sharp pain right after a fall, twist, or hit
Swelling and bruising around the foot or ankle
Pain when you try to stand or walk
A foot that looks bent, crooked, or out of shape
causes: Falls, missteps, and hard twists of the ankle
Car crashes and other sudden impacts
Heavy objects dropped on the foot
Sports collisions and awkward landings from jumps
diagnose: We check where it hurts, how the foot moves, and how the skin looks. X-rays in our office show most breaks and how far the bone has shifted. If the break is in a tricky spot like the talus or heel, we may send you for a CT scan or MRI for a closer look.
treat: Many fractures heal without surgery when the bones are lined up well. You may wear a cast, a walking boot, or a stiff-soled shoe. Some breaks need crutches so the foot can rest for a few weeks. We may tape a broken toe to its neighbor to keep it steady. Physical therapy helps you regain strength and balance once the bone is healing.
more: Surgery may be needed when a bone has moved out of place, a joint is involved, or a break is slow to heal. Surgeons often use plates, screws, or pins to hold the pieces together while they mend.
recovery: Simple toe breaks often feel much better in about 4 to 8 weeks. Larger breaks in the heel, talus, or ankle may take 3 months or more, and some stiffness or swelling can last longer.
when: See a podiatrist soon if you cannot put weight on your foot, or if it is swollen, bruised, or looks out of place. Go to an emergency room first if a bone is poking through the skin or the foot is numb or very pale.

faqs.q: How do I know if it is a break or a sprain?
faqs.a: They can feel alike, so an X-ray is the best way to tell. Pain over a bone or trouble bearing weight makes a break more likely.

faqs.q: Can I walk on a broken toe?
faqs.a: Some people can, but walking may slow healing or shift the bone. Have it checked so we can tell you how much weight is safe.

title: Foot, Ankle & Toe Fractures (Fifth Metatarsal, Jones, Heel/Calcaneal, Talus, Navicular)

lead: A stress fracture is a tiny crack in a bone. It grows from repeated pressure, not from one big injury. In the foot, it often shows up in the metatarsals, the small sesamoid bones under the big toe, or the heel bone.

Runners, dancers, and people who suddenly do more walking or standing are often affected. The pain usually starts mild and slowly gets worse. Catching it early can keep a small crack from becoming a full break.
feels: Pain that builds during activity and eases with rest
A sore spot on the bone that hurts when pressed
Mild swelling on the top or bottom of the foot
Pain that starts to show up even at rest
causes: Adding miles or activity too fast
Worn-out shoes or hard training surfaces
Low bone strength or poor nutrition
Foot shape issues that overload one bone
diagnose: We ask about your activity, shoes, and recent changes, then press gently along the bones to find the sore spot. X-rays are used, but early cracks may not show at first. If we still suspect a stress fracture, an MRI can find it sooner.
treat: Rest from the activity that caused it is the most important step. We may place you in a walking boot or a stiff shoe, and sometimes crutches, to take pressure off the bone. Padding or orthotics can spread out the load once you are healing. Then we help you return to activity in small steps, often with physical therapy.
more: Most stress fractures heal without surgery. Surgery is sometimes used for bones that heal poorly, such as some sesamoid or fifth metatarsal cracks, or if a crack becomes a full break.
recovery: Many stress fractures need about 6 to 8 weeks to heal, and some take longer. Going back too soon is the most common reason they return.
when: See a podiatrist if foot pain keeps coming back with activity or you have a spot that hurts to touch. Do not keep training through it, because the crack can get worse.

faqs.q: Why did my X-ray look normal?
faqs.a: Small early cracks often do not show on X-rays. An MRI or a repeat X-ray a couple of weeks later may show what is going on.

faqs.q: Can I keep exercising?
faqs.a: Usually you can do low-impact options like swimming if they do not cause pain. We will tell you what is safe for your bone.

title: Stress Fractures (Metatarsal, Sesamoid, Calcaneal)

lead: The Lisfranc joint is the group of small bones and strong ligaments in the middle of your foot. It holds the arch together. A Lisfranc injury means those bones are broken, shifted, or the ligaments are torn.

This injury can happen from a twist while the foot is planted, a fall, or a crush. It is often mistaken for a simple sprain. Finding it early matters because unstable bones can lead to long-term arch pain.
feels: Pain and swelling across the top of the midfoot
Bruising on the bottom of the foot, in the arch
Pain when you stand on your toes or push off
Trouble walking, or a foot that feels unstable
causes: Twisting the foot while the toes are pointed down
Falls from a step or ladder
Car crashes and heavy objects landing on the foot
Sports tackles or a horse or bike accident
diagnose: We look for swelling, bruising in the arch, and pain when the midfoot is gently moved. X-rays are taken, sometimes while you stand, to see if the bones have spread apart. A CT scan or MRI may be used to see small breaks and torn ligaments.
treat: A mild Lisfranc sprain with stable bones may be treated with a cast or boot and no weight on the foot for several weeks. Crutches are usually needed. We recheck with X-rays to make sure the bones have not moved. After that, a firm shoe, arch support, and physical therapy help you walk normally again.
more: When the bones have shifted or the joint is unstable, surgery is often advised. The surgeon lines the bones up and holds them with screws or plates, and sometimes joins the bones together.
recovery: Healing often takes 2 to 4 months, and full return to sports may take longer. Some people have lasting stiffness or arch pain, especially after a serious injury.
when: See a podiatrist right away if you have midfoot swelling and pain after a twist or fall, especially with bruising on the sole. Do not wait it out, since a missed injury can get worse.

faqs.q: Is a Lisfranc injury just a bad sprain?
faqs.a: It can look like one, but it involves the joints and ligaments that hold your arch. That is why it needs a careful exam and imaging.

faqs.q: Will I get arthritis?
faqs.a: Some people do develop arthritis in the midfoot after this injury. Good alignment early on helps lower that risk.

title: Lisfranc Fractures & Dislocations

short: foot and ankle sprains and dislocations
lead: A sprain is a stretch or tear of a ligament, the tough band that connects bone to bone. A dislocation happens when a joint slips out of its normal place. Both can happen in the ankle, the midfoot, or the toes.
Ankle sprains are very common, especially in athletes and on uneven ground. Swelling and pain show up fast. Proper care helps prevent the ankle from staying weak and rolling again.
feels: Pain and swelling around the ankle or joint
Bruising that spreads across the foot
A joint that looks out of place or feels loose
Trouble putting weight on the foot
causes: Rolling the ankle on uneven ground or a curb
Landing awkwardly after a jump
Sports contact and sudden changes in direction
Falls, stairs, and high-impact accidents
diagnose: We check swelling, tender spots, and how stable the joint feels when we move it gently. X-rays help rule out a break or show a joint that is out of place. Ultrasound or MRI can show the ligaments if we need to see how badly they are torn.
treat: For sprains, we often use rest, ice, compression, and lifting the foot in the first days. A brace, boot, or tape keeps the joint steady while it heals. Physical therapy works on motion, strength, and balance, which helps prevent repeat sprains. A dislocated joint needs to be put back in place by a clinician before other care begins.
more: Surgery may be considered when a joint keeps giving way, a ligament is fully torn, or a dislocation cannot be held in place. The surgeon repairs or rebuilds the ligaments to make the joint stable.
recovery: Mild sprains often improve in 2 to 6 weeks. Severe sprains and dislocations can take 3 months or longer to feel fully solid.
when: See a podiatrist if swelling and pain do not ease in a few days, or if you cannot walk on the foot. Go to an emergency room right away if the joint looks out of place.

faqs.q: Why does my ankle keep rolling?
faqs.a: Ligaments that healed loose or muscles that lost strength can make the ankle unstable. A brace and therapy often help.

faqs.q: Should I wrap it or use a brace?
faqs.a: Compression can ease swelling early on. A brace gives better support while you walk, and we can pick one that fits your injury.

title: Foot & Ankle Dislocations and Sprains

lead: Turf toe is a sprain of the ligaments at the base of the big toe. It happens when the toe bends back too far. The joint that pushes you off the ground becomes sore and swollen.

It is most common in football, soccer, and dance, and on hard or flexible-soled footwear. Pain can start suddenly or build over time. Treating it early helps you avoid long-lasting stiffness in the toe.
feels: Pain and swelling at the base of the big toe
Pain when you push off or go up on your toes
Bruising under or around the big toe joint
A stiff toe that will not bend or straighten well
causes: Jamming the big toe while it is bent upward
Pushing off hard on turf or other firm ground
Thin, bendy shoes that offer little toe support
Repeated small injuries to the big toe joint
diagnose: We press around the big toe joint and test how far it moves and how strong it feels. X-rays help rule out a broken bone or shifted sesamoids. An MRI may be used if we think the ligaments are badly torn.
treat: Rest and ice help calm swelling early on. Taping the toe or using a stiff-soled shoe limits bending so the ligament can heal. A walking boot may be needed for a more serious sprain. Later, an orthotic with a stiff plate and physical therapy can help you return to running and jumping safely.
more: Most turf toe heals without surgery. Surgery may be an option if the joint is unstable, the sesamoid bones have moved, or pain lasts for many months.
recovery: A mild case may settle in 1 to 3 weeks. A severe sprain may take 2 to 3 months or more, and rushing back can cause a setback.
when: See a podiatrist if your big toe hurts to push off, swells, or bruises after an injury. Get help sooner if you cannot bear weight or the toe looks crooked.

faqs.q: Can I play through turf toe?
faqs.a: Playing on it can make the sprain worse and last longer. We can advise on tape or a shoe insert if you need to return early.

faqs.q: Why does my big toe still feel stiff?
faqs.a: Scar tissue and a tight joint can remain after the sprain settles. Gentle motion work and therapy often help.

title: Turf Toe

lead: Shin splints are pain along the inner edge of the shinbone. They happen when the muscles and tissue around the bone get irritated from repeated pounding. Other running injuries can affect the heel, arch, knee, or ankle.

Runners, dancers, and anyone who ramps up training too fast are often affected. The ache may start mild and grow with each run. Early care can keep a small problem from forcing you to stop for months.
feels: A dull ache or soreness along the shin
Pain that starts at the beginning of a run
Tenderness when you press along the inner shin
Aching that lingers after activity ends
causes: Doing too much, too soon, or too often
Running on hard surfaces or slanted roads
Old shoes that have lost cushion or support
Flat feet, high arches, or weak calf muscles
diagnose: We watch how you stand and walk, and sometimes how you run. We check your arches, ankles, and where the shin is sore. X-rays or an MRI may be used to rule out a stress fracture if the pain is sharp or focused on one spot.
treat: Lowering your mileage and giving the shin time to calm down is key. Ice, calf stretches, and strengthening exercises help. New shoes and custom orthotics can improve how your foot absorbs force. Physical therapy can fix weak spots and teach a smoother running form.
more: Surgery is rarely needed for shin splints. It is only considered for stubborn cases that do not respond to months of proper care, or when another cause like a bone problem is found.
recovery: Many people feel better in about 2 to 6 weeks of smart rest and rehab. A slow, planned return to running lowers the chance of flare-ups.
when: See a podiatrist if shin pain lasts more than a couple of weeks, hurts at night, or is sharp in one spot. Those signs can point to a stress fracture.

faqs.q: Should I stop running completely?
faqs.a: Not always. Cutting back and switching to low-impact exercise often works, but sharp or worsening pain means a full rest.

faqs.q: Do my shoes matter?
faqs.a: Yes. Worn shoes or a poor fit can add strain, and running shoes usually need replacing after several hundred miles.

title: Shin Splints & Running Injuries

short: crush injuries, puncture wounds, and foreign objects in the foot
lead: These are injuries where something hurts the foot from the outside. A crush injury comes from a heavy load. A puncture wound is a deep, narrow hole from a nail, glass, or sharp object. A foreign body is a piece of material like a splinter, glass, or metal left inside.
Even a small wound on the sole can push germs deep into the foot. Pain, swelling, and redness may build over days. Quick care lowers the chance of infection and helps protect bones and tendons.
feels: Pain, swelling, or bruising after a heavy blow
A small wound that hurts more each day
Redness, warmth, or drainage around the wound
A feeling that something is stuck in the skin
causes: Stepping on nails, glass, or thorns
Dropping heavy tools or equipment on the foot
Walking barefoot outdoors or in the yard
Workplace or car accidents that pin the foot
diagnose: We look closely at the wound, check feeling and blood flow, and ask when and how it happened. X-rays show broken bones and many objects like glass or metal. Ultrasound can find wood or plastic that X-rays may miss.
treat: We clean the wound well, and remove any object during a minor in-office procedure. Dead or dirty tissue may be trimmed away to help healing. We use dressings and wound care, and may advise a tetanus check and antibiotics when needed. For crush injuries, we control swelling and protect the foot with a boot or splint.
more: Surgery may be needed if bones are broken, the wound is deep, or an infection has spread. In serious crush injuries, a surgeon may repair bone, skin, or tendon.
recovery: A simple puncture may heal in 1 to 3 weeks with good care. Crush injuries with broken bones or skin damage can take months to recover.
when: See a podiatrist the same day for a puncture, a possible object in the foot, or a crush injury. Go to an emergency room for heavy bleeding, numbness, or a foot that looks pale or bluish.

faqs.q: Can I remove a piece of glass myself?
faqs.a: It is best not to dig for it. Digging can push it deeper or leave pieces behind, and we can find and remove it safely.

faqs.q: Do I need a tetanus shot?
faqs.a: Deep or dirty wounds often call for a tetanus check. We will ask about your last shot and advise you.

title: Crush Injuries, Puncture Wounds & Foreign Bodies

lead: A diabetic foot exam is a regular check of your skin, nerves, blood flow, and foot shape. High blood sugar can harm nerves and blood vessels over time. That makes small problems easy to miss and slow to heal.

People with diabetes, and others with poor feeling or circulation, benefit from routine visits. Most serious foot problems start small, like a blister or a dry crack. Regular exams help us catch trouble early.
feels: Often no symptoms at all, which is why exams matter
Numbness, tingling, or burning in the feet
Skin that is dry, cracked, or has new sores
Feet that feel cold, or toenails that thicken or change
causes: Long-term high blood sugar
Nerve damage that dulls the feeling of pain
Reduced blood flow to the legs and feet
Foot shape changes and poor-fitting shoes
diagnose: We look over your skin, nails, and toes for sores, calluses, and signs of infection. We test feeling with a light touch or a small tool, and check pulses to see how blood is flowing. If needed, we may order blood tests or circulation studies, or take X-rays.
treat: Care starts with a daily foot check, gentle washing, and good moisturizer, but not between the toes. We trim nails and calluses safely so you do not have to. Diabetic shoes, inserts, and orthotics reduce pressure on risky spots. We also teach you which signs mean call us right away.
more: Surgery is not part of a routine exam. If a deformity keeps causing sores, surgery may be discussed to reshape the foot and take pressure off the area.
recovery: Routine care is ongoing, not a one-time fix. Most people at higher risk do best with visits every few months, and we will suggest a schedule that fits you.
when: Book a visit if you have diabetes and have not had a foot exam this year. Come in quickly for any new sore, blister, color change, or swelling, even if it does not hurt.

faqs.q: How often should I have a foot exam?
faqs.a: At least once a year is a common guide, and more often if you have nerve loss or past foot sores. We will set a plan for you.

faqs.q: Why check my feet if they feel fine?
faqs.a: Nerve damage can hide pain, so a sore can grow without you feeling it. Exams find problems you cannot feel.

title: Diabetic Foot Exams & At-Risk Foot Care

lead: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy is nerve damage that mostly affects the feet and legs. It can cause pain, tingling, or a loss of feeling. Charcot foot is a serious problem where weak, numb bones and joints break down and the foot changes shape.
Neuropathy is common in people who have had diabetes for years. Charcot often begins quietly, with a warm, swollen foot that may not hurt much. Early care can protect the foot from lasting damage.
feels: Tingling, burning, or stabbing feelings in the feet
Numb feet that do not feel heat, cold, or pain
A foot that is red, warm, and swollen
An arch that slowly sinks or a foot that changes shape
causes: Long-term high blood sugar harming the nerves
Low feeling that hides small injuries
Repeated stress on numb bones and joints
Poor blood flow adding to nerve and bone damage
diagnose: We test how well you feel touch, vibration, and pressure, and check reflexes. For Charcot, we compare the warmth and swelling of both feet and look at foot shape. X-rays show bone changes, and an MRI may help when early Charcot or infection is hard to tell apart.
treat: For nerve symptoms, steady blood sugar control and daily foot checks are the base of care. We may suggest protective shoes and inserts for numb feet. Charcot needs strict protection, usually a cast or boot with no weight on the foot until it calms down. After that, custom bracing or shoes help protect the shape of the foot.
more: Surgery may be considered for Charcot when the foot is badly out of shape, unstable, or has repeated sores. Surgeons can realign and fuse bones, but this is done with great care.
recovery: Nerve symptoms often need ongoing management. Charcot usually takes several months of protection to settle, and lifelong special footwear is common.
when: See a podiatrist if your feet feel numb, burn, or tingle, or if one foot becomes warm, red, and swollen. Warm swelling with numbness should be looked at quickly, even without pain.

faqs.q: Can neuropathy be reversed?
faqs.a: Damage that has already happened often cannot be fully undone. Good blood sugar control can slow it and protect your feet.

faqs.q: Why is Charcot foot so hard to notice?
faqs.a: Numb feet may not hurt even when bones are breaking down. Warmth and swelling are often the first signs.

title: Diabetic Peripheral Neuropathy & Charcot Foot

lead: A foot ulcer is an open sore that does not heal the way a normal cut would. It can be shallow or deep. Ulcers may be linked to diabetes, nerve damage, pressure, or poor blood flow in the arteries or veins.
Ulcers often form on the bottom of the foot, the heels, or the toes. Many people do not feel them at first. Treating an ulcer early lowers the risk of infection and serious complications.
feels: An open sore or blister that will not close
Drainage, odor, or crusting on a wound
Red, warm, or swollen skin around the sore
Little or no pain, even with a deep wound
causes: Pressure or rubbing on numb areas of the foot
Poor blood flow from blocked leg arteries
Weak leg veins that cause swelling and skin breakdown
Ill-fitting shoes and hard calluses
diagnose: We measure and photograph the sore, note its depth, and check for infection. We check pulses and skin color to see how well blood flows. X-rays or an MRI can show whether bone is involved, and we may order circulation tests or blood tests.
treat: The main goals are to take pressure off the sore and keep it clean and moist. We remove dead tissue during minor in-office procedures and use dressings picked for your wound type. Offloading with a boot, cast, or special shoe is often key. If blood flow is the problem, we work with vascular teams. Compression is used for vein-related ulcers when circulation is safe for it.
more: Surgery may help when a bone deformity keeps causing pressure, when infection is deep, or when blood flow needs to be restored. A vascular procedure may be needed before a wound can heal.
recovery: Healing can take several weeks to several months, depending on the cause and your health. Ulcers can return, so long-term shoes and checks matter.
when: See a podiatrist as soon as you notice an open sore, especially if you have diabetes or poor circulation. Seek urgent care for spreading redness, fever, or a foul smell.

faqs.q: Why won't my sore heal?
faqs.a: Pressure, poor blood flow, infection, or high blood sugar can all slow healing. We look for the cause so treatment fits it.

faqs.q: Can I keep walking on it?
faqs.a: Walking on an ulcer can keep it open. We will give you an offloading device so you can move with less pressure.

title: Foot Ulcers (Diabetic, Neuropathic, Pressure, Arterial, Venous)

lead: A chronic wound is a sore that has not healed after several weeks or keeps coming back. Limb preservation is care that aims to save your foot or leg and keep you walking. It uses a team approach to find and fix what is blocking healing.

Wounds that stay open are often tied to diabetes, poor circulation, infection, or constant pressure. The longer they stay open, the higher the risk of serious trouble. Fast attention gives you the best chance to keep your limb.
feels: A wound that has not improved in 2 to 4 weeks
Skin that is dark, pale, or very cold around a sore
Increasing pain, drainage, or swelling
New wounds appearing in the same spot
causes: Poor blood flow that starves the wound of oxygen
Diabetes and uncontrolled blood sugar
Ongoing pressure on the same part of the foot
Infection deep in the tissue or bone
diagnose: We review your health history and look closely at the wound and the skin around it. We check pulses and may order circulation tests to see if blood flow is enough to heal. X-rays or an MRI look for bone infection, and blood tests can point to infection or other health issues.
treat: We clear dead tissue with minor in-office procedures and choose dressings that fit the wound. Offloading boots and casts take pressure off the area. We treat infection and work with your doctors on blood sugar, nutrition, and circulation. Compression, wound care, and shockwave therapy may be used in some cases.
more: When wounds do not respond, surgery may be used to fix blood flow, clear infected bone, or reshape a foot that keeps breaking down. Removing part of the foot is a last resort, and the goal is always to keep as much of the foot as safely possible.
recovery: Chronic wounds can take weeks to many months to close. Progress is usually slow and steady, and staying on your plan matters a great deal.
when: See a podiatrist if a sore has not started to heal within 2 weeks. Go quickly for black or dying skin, spreading redness, or fever.

faqs.q: What does limb preservation mean?
faqs.a: It means a team works to save your foot and keep you walking. It often includes wound care, circulation checks, and infection control.

faqs.q: Will I lose my foot?
faqs.a: Many people keep their foot with early, steady care. The sooner a wound is treated, the better the outlook.

title: Chronic Non-Healing Wounds & Limb Preservation

lead: A foot infection happens when germs get into the skin or deeper tissue. Cellulitis is an infection of the skin and the layer below it. An abscess is a pocket of pus, and osteomyelitis is an infection in the bone.
Cuts, cracks, ingrown nails, and sores can let germs in. People with diabetes or poor circulation are at higher risk. Infections can spread fast, so quick treatment is important.
feels: Red, warm, swollen, or tender skin
A pocket of pus or a painful lump
Drainage or a bad smell from a wound
Fever, chills, or red streaks moving up the leg
causes: Cuts, cracks, blisters, and puncture wounds
Ingrown toenails and athlete's foot
Open ulcers that stay uncovered
A weakened immune system or poor blood flow
diagnose: We examine the skin for redness, warmth, swelling, and drainage. We may take a sample from a wound to find the germ, and order blood tests. X-rays or an MRI can show whether the infection has reached the bone.
treat: Treatment often includes prescription antibiotics matched to the germ. For an abscess, we drain the pocket during a minor in-office procedure and clean the area. We use wound care and rest, and raise the foot to reduce swelling. Deep or spreading infections may need care in the hospital with medicine given through a vein.
more: Surgery may be needed to clean out infected tissue or bone, especially with osteomyelitis or a deep abscess. Removing infected bone can help the infection clear and protect the rest of the foot.
recovery: Skin infections often improve in days to a couple of weeks. Bone infections can need many weeks of treatment and follow-up.
when: See a podiatrist right away for redness, warmth, pus, or a wound that looks worse each day. Go to an emergency room for fever, red streaks, confusion, or fast-spreading redness.

faqs.q: Is cellulitis contagious?
faqs.a: It usually does not spread from person to person. It is a skin infection that needs treatment so it does not spread inside your body.

faqs.q: Why do I need X-rays for a skin infection?
faqs.a: They can show gas, foreign objects, or bone changes. That helps us know if the infection is deeper than it looks.

title: Foot Infections, Cellulitis, Abscesses & Osteomyelitis

short: peripheral arterial disease and poor circulation
lead: Peripheral arterial disease, or PAD, means the arteries in the legs have narrowed. Less blood reaches the feet, so they get less oxygen and heal slowly. It is a common cause of poor circulation.

PAD is more likely in people who smoke or have diabetes, high blood pressure, or high cholesterol. It often starts with leg cramps when walking. Finding it early lowers the chance of wounds and helps protect your heart too.
feels: Leg or calf cramps when walking that ease with rest
Cold, pale, or bluish feet and toes
Sores on the feet or toes that heal slowly
Foot pain at night that eases when the foot hangs down
causes: Fatty buildup that narrows the leg arteries
Smoking and tobacco use
Diabetes, high blood pressure, and high cholesterol
Older age and a family history of artery disease
diagnose: We check pulses in your feet, skin color and temperature, and hair and nail changes. We may do simple blood pressure tests in the ankle and arm to compare blood flow. Ultrasound of the arteries or other imaging may be advised, and we may refer you to a vascular specialist.
treat: Care often starts with lifestyle steps, like quitting smoking and a walking program. Your doctors may manage blood pressure, cholesterol, and blood sugar. We protect your feet with good shoes, wound care, and daily checks. If sores are present, we treat them and coordinate with vascular care.
more: When blood flow is very low, a vascular specialist may open or bypass the blocked arteries. This can help wounds heal and ease pain.
recovery: PAD is a long-term condition that is managed, not cured. Walking programs can take a few months to show benefit, and wounds may heal slowly.
when: See a podiatrist if you have leg cramps with walking, cold feet, or sores that will not heal. Get urgent help for a sudden cold, pale, or very painful foot.

faqs.q: Is leg pain when walking normal with age?
faqs.a: It is common, but it should not be brushed off. Cramps that ease with rest can be a sign of PAD.

faqs.q: Does walking help PAD?
faqs.a: Regular walking, planned with your care team, can improve how far you can go. Stop and rest when pain starts, then try again.

title: Peripheral Arterial Disease (PAD) & Poor Circulation

lead: Swelling happens when extra fluid collects in the tissues of the legs and feet. This is called edema. Lymphedema is a longer-lasting kind caused by a problem in the lymph system, which normally drains fluid.
Swelling can come from standing all day, heart or vein problems, injury, or some medicines. It may go up and down or stay. Finding the cause matters, since some causes are serious.
feels: Puffy feet, ankles, or legs that leave a dent
Shoes, socks, or rings that feel tight
Skin that looks stretched, shiny, or thick
A heavy, tired, or achy feeling in the legs
causes: Weak leg veins that let fluid pool
Heart, kidney, or liver conditions
Injury, surgery, or damage to the lymph system
Long hours of standing or sitting, and some medicines
diagnose: We check which areas are swollen, whether one or both legs are involved, and how the skin looks. We press on the skin and check pulses and the veins. Ultrasound can look for blood clots or vein problems, and blood tests may point to other causes.
treat: Treatment depends on the cause. Raising the legs, moving often, and wearing compression stockings can help move fluid. We check that circulation is safe before advising compression. Good skin care prevents cracks and infection, and we may refer you to a therapist trained in lymph drainage. We also work with your other doctors when a heart or kidney problem is involved.
more: Surgery is rarely the first choice for swelling. Vein procedures may help some vein problems, and lymphedema surgery is used only in select cases.
recovery: Swelling from a short-term cause often eases in days to weeks. Long-term swelling, like lymphedema, is usually managed over time rather than cured.
when: See a podiatrist if swelling lasts more than a week, keeps returning, or comes with skin changes or sores. Seek urgent care if one leg swells suddenly with pain, or if you have trouble breathing.

faqs.q: Is a swollen leg a blood clot?
faqs.a: It can be, especially if one leg swells fast and hurts. That needs urgent care, so do not wait.

faqs.q: Do compression stockings help?
faqs.a: They often do for vein-related swelling. We check your circulation first so they are safe for you.

title: Leg and Foot Swelling, Edema & Lymphedema

short: tarsal tunnel syndrome and nerve pain in the feet
lead: Tarsal tunnel syndrome happens when the tibial nerve gets squeezed as it passes along the inner ankle. It works a bit like carpal tunnel in the wrist. The pressure can make the nerve send odd signals to the foot.

It often shows up in people with flat feet, past ankle injuries, or swelling around the ankle. Most people notice burning, tingling, or numbness in the sole. Getting checked early can protect the nerve from lasting irritation.
feels: Burning or tingling in the sole, heel, or toes
Numbness that may spread along the inner ankle
Shooting or electric pain that often gets worse at night
Symptoms that flare after long standing or walking
causes: Flat feet that stretch the nerve
Past ankle sprains or fractures
Swelling or a cyst near the ankle
Tight or ill-fitting shoes
diagnose: We ask about your symptoms and gently tap along the nerve to see if it causes tingling. We also look at your foot shape and how you walk. X-rays, ultrasound, or an MRI referral can check for bone problems, cysts, or other growths. In some cases we may suggest nerve testing or blood tests to look for other causes of numbness.
treat: Rest and changes in activity can calm the nerve. Supportive shoes and custom orthotics may ease the strain from flat feet. Bracing, taping, or a short time in a boot can limit motion around the ankle. Some people benefit from injections to reduce swelling or from physical therapy to improve movement and strength.
more: Surgery may be talked about if the nerve stays pinched and other care has not helped. The goal is to release the tight tissue or remove whatever is pressing on the nerve.
recovery: Mild cases may improve over several weeks to a few months with care. If surgery is needed, recovery can take a few months, and results vary.
when: See a podiatrist if burning or numbness lasts more than a couple of weeks. Come in sooner if you feel weakness, if pain wakes you at night, or if you have diabetes.

faqs.q: Is burning in my feet always from the tarsal tunnel?
faqs.a: No. Nerve pain in the feet can also come from diabetes, back problems, or other causes. An exam helps sort out which one it is.

faqs.q: Can shoes make tarsal tunnel worse?
faqs.a: Yes, tight shoes or shoes with little support can add pressure near the ankle. Better fit and support often help.

title: Tarsal Tunnel Syndrome, Nerve Entrapment, Burning Feet & Numbness

lead: Corns and calluses are thick, hard patches of skin that form where your foot rubs or takes extra pressure. Cracked heels are dry, thick skin that splits open at the back of the foot.
These problems are common in adults and active people. You may see rough skin at first, then feel soreness when you walk. Care early can keep small cracks from becoming deep or painful.
feels: Hard, yellowish patches on the toes or ball of the foot
Small, painful bumps that hurt when pressed
Dry, flaky skin around the heel edge
Deep cracks that sting or sometimes bleed
causes: Shoes that rub, pinch, or fit too tightly
Toe shape problems like hammertoes
Walking barefoot or wearing open backed shoes
Very dry skin or long periods of standing
diagnose: We look at the thick skin and find where the pressure is coming from. We check your toe shape, gait, and shoes. If a bump does not look like a normal corn, we may look more closely to rule out other skin growths. X-rays can help when a bone shape may be adding pressure.
treat: We can gently trim thick skin in the office, which often brings quick relief. Moisturizing creams with softening ingredients help keep heels supple. Padding, toe spacers, and roomier shoes reduce rubbing. Custom orthotics can spread pressure more evenly across the foot. Please do not cut corns at home or use strong acid pads if you have diabetes or poor circulation.
more: Surgery is rarely needed. If a bone shape keeps causing painful corns, a small procedure to reshape the area may be an option.
recovery: After trimming, most people feel better right away. Skin can build up again if the cause stays the same, so ongoing care over weeks and months helps.
when: See a podiatrist if a corn or callus hurts, bleeds, or looks red or warm. Come in soon for deep heel cracks, or right away if you have diabetes.

faqs.q: Why do my corns keep coming back?
faqs.a: The pressure that made them is usually still there. Changing shoes or using padding and orthotics can help.

faqs.q: Can I use a pumice stone on my heels?
faqs.a: Gentle use after a shower is fine for most people. Skip it if you have diabetes or numb feet, and ask us first.

title: Corns, Calluses & Cracked Heels

lead: Plantar warts are small growths on the bottom of the foot caused by a virus. The virus enters through tiny breaks in the skin. Pressure from walking can push the wart inward, so it may look flat.
Children, teens, and people who use shared pools or locker rooms often get them. They can be tender when you walk or stand. Treating them early can stop them from spreading or growing larger.
feels: A rough spot that looks like a callus
Tiny black dots inside the growth
Pain when you squeeze the sides of the spot
Soreness when you stand or walk
causes: A virus that spreads on damp floors
Tiny cuts or cracks in the skin
Walking barefoot in pools or locker rooms
A weaker immune response in some people
diagnose: We look closely at the spot and gently trim the top layer to see the tiny dark dots that mark a wart. This helps us tell it apart from a callus or corn. Imaging is not usually needed, but we may use it if something looks unusual.
treat: Warts can be stubborn, so we often use a step by step plan. This may include medicated treatments applied in the office, gentle removal of thick skin, and protective padding. Some warts need minor in-office procedures. Keep the area clean and dry, wear sandals in public wet areas, and do not share towels or shoes.
more: Surgery is rarely needed. A minor in-office procedure may be used for warts that do not respond to other care.
recovery: Many warts clear over weeks to several months, and some need repeat visits. They can return, so ongoing prevention matters.
when: See a podiatrist if a spot on your foot hurts, spreads, or does not go away. Come in sooner if you have diabetes, poor circulation, or a weak immune system.

faqs.q: Are plantar warts contagious?
faqs.a: Yes, the virus can spread through shared damp surfaces. Cover the wart and avoid walking barefoot in public places.

faqs.q: Should I cut the wart off myself?
faqs.a: No. Cutting it can spread the virus and cause infection. Let us treat it safely.

title: Plantar Warts

lead: Athlete's foot is a fungal infection of the skin on the feet. It often starts between the toes and can spread to the sole or sides of the foot. The fungus grows best in warm, damp places.
It is common in teens, active people, and anyone whose feet stay sweaty. You may notice itching, peeling, or red skin. Treating it early keeps it from spreading to the nails or other people.
feels: Itchy, burning skin between the toes
Peeling or cracked skin that looks white and soft
Dry, scaly skin along the sole and sides
Small blisters that may leak fluid
causes: Sweaty feet in closed shoes
Damp socks worn for long periods
Walking barefoot in locker rooms or pools
Sharing towels, mats, or shoes
diagnose: We look at the pattern of the rash and ask how long you have had it. Other skin problems can look similar, such as eczema or contact rashes. If needed, we can gently scrape a small sample of skin to check for fungus.
treat: Antifungal creams or sprays are the main treatment, and stronger options may be prescribed when needed. Keep feet dry, change socks often, and let shoes air out between wears. Wear sandals in public showers. Finish the full treatment plan, even after the itching stops, so the fungus does not return.
more: Surgery is not part of treating athlete's foot. Treatment focuses on medicine and keeping the skin dry.
recovery: Many people feel better within a couple of weeks, but the skin may need longer to fully heal. It can come back if damp habits continue.
when: See a podiatrist if the rash lasts more than a couple of weeks or keeps coming back. Come in promptly if you see redness, swelling, or pus, or if you have diabetes.

faqs.q: Can athlete's foot spread to my toenails?
faqs.a: Yes, the fungus can move into the nails over time. Treating the skin early lowers that risk.

faqs.q: Should I throw away my old shoes?
faqs.a: Not always. Airing them out, using antifungal powder, and washing socks in hot water can help.

title: Athlete's Foot

lead: A ganglion is a soft, fluid filled lump that grows near a joint or tendon. On the foot, it often appears on the top of the foot or near the ankle. The lump feels like a small firm bubble under the skin.
Many are painless, but some press on nerves or rub against shoes. People usually come in because they notice a lump that changes in size. Having it checked helps make sure it is what it seems.
feels: A round, smooth lump under the skin
Aching or pressure when shoes rub the spot
Tingling if the lump presses on a nerve
A lump that grows or shrinks over time
causes: Wear and strain on a joint or tendon
Past injury to the area
Repeated stress from activity
Often no clear cause is found
diagnose: We feel the lump and check whether it moves and how firm it is. Ultrasound is useful because it can show fluid inside. An X-ray may look at nearby bones, and an MRI referral can help with deeper or unclear lumps.
treat: If a ganglion does not bother you, we may simply watch it. Shoe changes or padding can take pressure off the area. In some cases, we can drain the fluid in the office, though the lump can return. Rest and limiting repeated strain may also help. Please do not try to pop it at home.
more: If the cyst keeps returning or causes ongoing pain, surgery to remove it may be considered. This also removes the stalk that connects it to the joint or tendon.
recovery: After draining, you can usually return to normal activity quickly, but the lump may come back. After surgery, expect a few weeks of healing, sometimes longer.
when: See a podiatrist for any new lump on your foot, especially if it grows, hurts, or changes color. Come in sooner if you feel numbness or the lump makes shoes hard to wear.

faqs.q: Is a ganglion cancer?
faqs.a: Ganglions are not cancer. Still, other lumps can look similar, so it is smart to have new lumps checked.

faqs.q: Will it go away on its own?
faqs.a: Some shrink or disappear, while others stay or come back. We can talk through options if it bothers you.

title: Cysts & Ganglions

lead: An ingrown toenail happens when the edge of the nail grows into the skin beside it. This most often affects the big toe. The skin can become sore, swollen, and sometimes infected.
Teens and adults both get them, and they can start from small daily habits. Pain often builds slowly. Early care can help you avoid infection and stay comfortable in your shoes.
feels: Tenderness along the side of the nail
Redness and swelling around the toe
Pain when a shoe or sock touches the toe
Drainage or a bad smell if infected
causes: Cutting nails too short or curved at the edges
Shoes that squeeze the toes
Stubbing or dropping something on the toe
Curved nails that run in families
diagnose: We look at the nail edge and the skin around it, and check for signs of infection. The diagnosis is usually clear from the exam. If a bone problem or deep infection is a concern, an X-ray may be used.
treat: For mild cases, we may show you how to soak the toe and lift the nail edge gently. Roomier shoes and correct nail trimming help. If there is infection, we may prescribe treatment for it. For a painful nail, a minor in-office procedure can remove the part of the nail that is digging in, often after numbing the toe.
more: If the nail keeps coming back, a minor procedure can treat the nail edge so that part is less likely to grow again. This is done in the office in many cases.
recovery: After a minor procedure, most people feel much better within days and heal in a few weeks. Your toe may need simple dressing changes during that time.
when: See a podiatrist if the toe is very painful, red, or draining. Come in right away if you have diabetes or poor circulation, even if the toe seems mildly sore.

faqs.q: Can I fix an ingrown nail at home?
faqs.a: Mild cases can improve with warm soaks and better shoes. Do not dig at the nail, especially if it looks infected.

faqs.q: Will the nail grow back normally?
faqs.a: In most cases, yes. If a portion was treated to stop regrowth, that edge may stay narrower.

title: Ingrown Toenails

lead: Toenail fungus is an infection that grows in and under the nail. Over time, the nail can change color and become thick or brittle. It spreads slowly and can affect one nail or several.
It is more common as we get older and in people who have athlete's foot. Many people first notice how the nail looks. Early care may make treatment easier.
feels: Yellow, white, or brown color in the nail
Nails that thicken and are hard to trim
Crumbly or brittle nail edges
Slight odor or discomfort in shoes
causes: Fungus that enters through tiny nail cracks
Athlete's foot on the same foot
Warm, damp, closed shoes
Walking barefoot in public wet areas
diagnose: We examine the nail and ask how long it has looked this way. Other problems like psoriasis, injury, or nail damage can look alike. To confirm fungus, we may take a small nail clipping to test.
treat: Treatment depends on how much of the nail is affected. Options include medicated nail products, prescription treatment, and careful trimming and thinning of the nail. Keeping feet dry and switching shoes daily helps. Treating athlete's foot at the same time lowers the chance of it returning.
more: Surgery is rarely used. In severe or painful cases, a minor procedure may be considered to remove part of the nail.
recovery: Nails grow slowly, so it can take many months to see clear new growth. Fungus can return, and results vary from person to person.
when: See a podiatrist if a nail turns thick, discolored, or painful. Come in soon if you have diabetes, since nail problems can lead to skin breakdown.

faqs.q: Why does treatment take so long?
faqs.a: Toenails grow slowly, so the healthy nail needs many months to replace the damaged part.

faqs.q: Can nail polish hide the fungus?
faqs.a: Polish may hide the look but does not treat it. It can also trap moisture, so ask us before using it.

title: Toenail Fungus

lead: A dystrophic nail is one that has changed in shape, thickness, or texture. It may look ridged, crumbly, curved, or very thick. Fungus is one cause, but it is not the only one.

People often notice these nails after an injury or as they get older. The nails can be hard to trim and may press on the skin inside shoes. A proper check helps us find the cause and choose the right care.
feels: Nails that are thick, rough, or hard to cut
Ridges, grooves, or a curled shape
Pain from the nail pressing on the toe
A dull, cloudy, or dark look
causes: Past injury or repeated pressure from shoes
Fungal infection
Skin conditions such as psoriasis
Poor circulation or getting older
diagnose: We look at every affected nail and ask about injuries, health conditions, and shoes. We may take a small nail sample to test for fungus. If we suspect a bone or circulation issue, imaging or extra testing can help.
treat: Regular gentle trimming and thinning of the nail can relieve pressure and pain. If fungus is present, we treat it as well. Padding, roomy shoes, and toe protection can reduce rubbing. Good nail care at home, done softly, also helps.
more: Surgery is not often needed. If a nail stays painful or keeps causing problems, a minor procedure to remove part or all of the nail may be discussed.
recovery: Nail changes can take many months to grow out, and some nails never look fully normal. Comfort usually improves sooner than looks.
when: See a podiatrist if a nail changes shape or color, or if it hurts. Come in sooner if you have diabetes or notice redness, swelling, or an open sore near the nail.

faqs.q: Is a thick nail always fungus?
faqs.a: No. Injury, skin conditions, and age can also cause thick nails. Testing shows which cause is behind it.

faqs.q: Will my nail ever look normal again?
faqs.a: It may improve, especially if the cause is treated. Long term damage can leave some changes behind.

title: Thickened & Dystrophic Nails

lead: A subungual hematoma is a collection of blood trapped beneath a nail. It usually follows a hit or a crush injury to the toe. The nail may turn red, purple, or black.
Runners, hikers, and people who drop things on their feet get this often. The pressure from the trapped blood can throb. Checking it soon can ease pain and rule out a broken bone.
feels: A dark red, purple, or black spot under the nail
Throbbing pain right after an injury
Pressure or tenderness when you touch the toe
A nail that feels loose or looks lifted
causes: Dropping a heavy object on the toe
Stubbing the toe hard
Toes hitting the front of tight shoes
Repeated pounding during running or hiking
diagnose: We ask how the injury happened and look at how much of the nail is involved. An X-ray is often done to check for a broken toe bone. We also make sure the dark spot is from injury and not something else, especially if there was no clear injury.
treat: For a painful, fresh bleed, we can release the pressure with a minor in-office procedure, which often brings quick relief. Smaller spots may just need rest, icing, and roomy shoes. We may protect the nail with a dressing. If the nail lifts, we help keep the area clean.
more: Surgery is rarely needed. If the nail bed is cut or badly damaged, it may need repair or nail removal.
recovery: Pain often eases within days after pressure is released. The dark mark grows out slowly over several months as the nail replaces itself.
when: See a podiatrist soon after a toe injury with strong pain, swelling, or a dark nail. Come in right away if the toe looks bent, the skin is cut, or you have diabetes.

faqs.q: Will I lose the nail?
faqs.a: Sometimes. If the nail loosens, a new one usually grows back over several months.

faqs.q: Could a dark spot under the nail be something else?
faqs.a: Yes. A dark spot with no injury should be checked, since other skin problems can look similar.

title: Subungual Hematoma (Blood Under the Nail)

lead: Flat feet in children means the inner arch is low or seems to disappear when the child stands. Many babies and toddlers have flat feet because their arches are still forming. Most children's arches develop as they grow.
Some kids have flat feet that do not cause any trouble. Others may get tired legs, sore feet, or clumsy walking. A check helps tell normal growth from a foot that needs more support.
feels: Feet that look flat when standing
Tired or achy feet and legs after play
Shoes wearing down on the inner edge
Ankles that roll inward when walking
causes: Normal foot growth in young children
Loose joints and flexible ligaments
Family history of flat feet
A stiff foot from a joint condition
diagnose: We watch your child stand, walk, and rise up on their toes to see if an arch appears. We also check how flexible the foot is. X-rays can help if the foot is stiff, painful, or looks different than expected.
treat: Most flexible flat feet need no treatment. If your child has pain, supportive shoes and custom orthotics may help. Stretching and strengthening exercises with physical therapy can also support the foot. We may suggest limiting long barefoot walks on hard floors if the feet ache.
more: Surgery is rarely needed in children. It may be considered only for stiff or painful flat feet that do not improve with other care.
recovery: Many children outgrow flexible flat feet or feel fine as they grow. When treatment is needed, comfort often improves over weeks to months.
when: See a podiatrist if your child limps, complains of foot pain, or avoids play. Come in sooner if the foot is stiff or one foot looks very different from the other.

faqs.q: Will my child's arch develop on its own?
faqs.a: In many children it does, as the foot grows and muscles strengthen. We can check if it needs support.

faqs.q: Do flat feet stop kids from playing sports?
faqs.a: Most kids with flexible flat feet play sports well. If there is pain, we can help find the right support.

title: Pediatric Flat Feet

lead: Intoeing means a child's toes point inward when walking. Out-toeing means the toes point outward. Both are common while children grow, and they often come from how the bones or legs are lined up.
Parents may notice tripping or an unusual walk. Most cases improve over time without treatment. A check helps make sure nothing more needs attention.
feels: Toes pointing in or out when walking
Frequent tripping or stumbling
Knees or feet that turn in when sitting
A walking pattern that looks uneven
causes: Twisting of the shin bone
Twisting of the thigh bone
Curved foot shape from the womb position
Sitting in positions that twist the legs
diagnose: We watch your child walk and measure how the legs and feet turn. We check the hips, thighs, shins, and feet to find where the twist comes from. X-rays are not usually needed, but we may use them if something looks unusual or the twist is severe.
treat: Most children improve with growth, so we often watch and recheck over time. We may suggest sitting positions that are gentler on the legs. Some children benefit from stretching, exercises, or supportive shoes. Special braces are rarely used and only when they fit the child's needs.
more: Surgery is very rarely needed. It may be considered for a severe twist that does not improve as the child grows and affects daily life.
recovery: Many children improve gradually over months to years. Follow up visits help track how the legs are growing.
when: See a podiatrist if your child trips often, has pain, or if one foot turns more than the other. Come in soon if the twist gets worse or appears after age eight.

faqs.q: Should we make our child change how they sit?
faqs.a: Sitting cross legged or on the heels can help. Avoid forcing positions, and ask us for tips that fit your child.

faqs.q: Is intoeing painful?
faqs.a: Usually not. Pain is a reason to have your child checked.

title: Intoeing & Out-Toeing

lead: A bunion is a bump at the base of the big toe where the toe leans toward the others. A hammertoe is a toe that bends at the middle joint. Children and teens can get both, though it is less common than in adults.
These often run in families. Kids may say shoes hurt or that a toe looks bent. Early care can ease discomfort and help protect growing feet.
feels: A bump on the inside of the big toe joint
A toe that curls or stays bent
Redness or rubbing where shoes press
Foot pain during sports or long days
causes: Family history of bunions or bent toes
Flat feet or loose joints
Shoes that are too narrow or short
Muscle imbalance in the foot
diagnose: We look at the toe shape, how the joints move, and where the shoes rub. We watch how your child walks. X-rays show the bones and growth plates, which helps us judge how severe the shape is and how the foot may change.
treat: We start with roomy, well fitting shoes and padding or toe spacers. Custom orthotics can help guide the foot when it is rolling in. Stretching and exercises may improve toe movement. Ice and rest can calm sore spots, and we recheck as your child grows.
more: Surgery is rarely done in children, since the feet are still growing. It may be considered in teens with severe pain that does not improve with other care.
recovery: Comfort often improves within weeks with better shoes and support. Bunions and bent toes may still change with growth, so follow up matters.
when: See a podiatrist if your child has ongoing toe pain, sores from shoe rubbing, or a bump that is growing. Come in sooner if the toe is stiff or red.

faqs.q: Will my child's bunion get worse?
faqs.a: It can, especially if it runs in the family. Good shoes and support can help ease symptoms.

faqs.q: Do hammertoes fix themselves?
faqs.a: Flexible ones may improve with care. Stiff toes tend to need more attention.

title: Pediatric Bunions & Hammertoes

lead: Congenital foot deformities are differences in foot shape that a baby is born with. Examples include clubfoot, where the foot turns inward, and other twisted or curved feet. Some are mild, and some need treatment soon after birth.
Parents often see these at birth or in early checkups. Starting care early gives the foot the best chance to move and grow well. Our team works with your child's pediatric doctors to plan care.
feels: A foot that turns in, out, or points down
A foot that looks curved or bent
A stiff foot that does not move freely
Differences between the two feet
causes: Growth differences before birth
Family history of foot conditions
Baby's position in the womb
Underlying conditions affecting muscles or nerves
diagnose: We examine the foot and ankle, checking shape, movement, and stiffness. We compare it to the other foot and look at the legs and hips as well. X-rays or ultrasound may be used to see the bones and joints, and other imaging can be arranged when needed.
treat: Many conditions begin with gentle stretching and casting, done in a series over several weeks. Bracing is often used afterward to help hold the corrected position. Physical therapy and shoe or orthotic support may also help. Parents play a big role by following the brace schedule.
more: Some children need surgery if the foot does not respond to other care. This may involve releasing tight tissue or adjusting tendons, and your child's team will explain the plan.
recovery: Care often lasts through early childhood, with follow up as the child grows. Results vary, and some children need ongoing bracing or checkups.
when: See a podiatrist as soon as you notice an unusual foot shape in a newborn or baby. Early visits give more treatment choices.

faqs.q: Is a foot deformity caused by something I did?
faqs.a: No. These conditions are not caused by something a parent did. Many have no clear cause.

faqs.q: Can my child walk normally after treatment?
faqs.a: Many children walk and play well with care. We will talk about what to expect for your child's foot.

title: Congenital Foot Deformities
